However, we acknowledge that our ebullition evidence is a gross observation, as the pathway has been reported in several lakes in cold months (Walter, Zimov, Chanton, Verbyla, & Chapin, 2006; Wik, Crill, Bastviken, Danielsson, & Norbäck, 2011). In our study, we exclusively sampled on 1 day each month, which is not sufficient to accurately estimate this emission pathway. In the future, higher temporal resolution of sampling (by diurnal sampling, sampling several days per month and spatial analysis) is required to reduce uncertainties in CH₄ ebullition from aquatic ecosystems, as previously recommended by Wik, Thornton, et al. (2016). However, other methods used in the literature contain large uncertainties; DelSontro et al. (2011) indicated that the acoustic technology has large coefficients of variation that exceed 100%, while the classic randomised bubble trap method is highly biased and underestimates results (Walter Anthony & Anthony, 2013). Newer gas analysers and the combination with established techniques may help to determine CH₄ diffusion and ebullition in freshwater ecosystems. Zhao et al. (2015) suggested such a method as a tool for assessing diffusion and ebullition, while Grasset et al. (2016) was one of the first studies to include ebullition data from these newer gas analysers. In the context of CO₂, Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle can be classified as an acidic lake, in which CO₂ is the major inorganic carbon species (Cole & Prairie, 2009) and where the availability of allochthonous and autochthonous inorganic carbon is in some ecosystems a very important driver of CO₂ emissions to the atmosphere (Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). During turnover events, with the exception of spring in the SW basin, peaks of CO₂ fluxes were detected jointly with high CO₂ stored in the water column. The surplus CO₂ for both basins likely did not completely originate from surficial (0–20 cm, data not shown) sediments (1.0 ± 0.5 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average), as stored quantities were one order of magnitude lower than the mass of CO₂ emitted (13.0 ± 4.6 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average) and dissolved in the water column (9.3 ± 4.3 g C/m², mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This suggests inputs of CO₂ directly from external sources of inorganic carbon and indirectly from mineralisation of internal or external DOC (Brothers et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2018; Maberly et al., 2013; Tank et al., 2018; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). The reduction in DOC in the NE basin potentially accounted for the 41% reduction in total annual CO₂ emissions. Moreover, CH₄ emissions decreased to a similar extent (53%), but cannot, as previously discussed, be adequately explained by the reduced availability of DOC to the pelagic community. Ducharme-Riel, Vachon, Del Giorgio, and Prairie (2015) remarked on the complexity of lake dynamics since interaction between physical and biological factors regulates CO₂ dynamics. Sources of CO₂ and contributions by different sources need to be elucidated (Drake et al., 2018; Engel et al., 2018; Tank et al., 2018). It is important to note that we could not observe any CO₂ ebullition with the new gas analyser used in this study, but we acknowledge that our device was not sensitive enough to confirm CO₂ in bubbles for several reasons: (a) CO₂ is highly soluble in water, and therefore, bubbles trapped in sediments might have had low CO₂ concentration; (b) the remaining CO₂ concentration in gas bubbles could have been re-dissolved through the water column before bubbles were emitted to the atmosphere (McGinnis et al., 2011); (c) there was a high CO₂ concentration inside the chamber (atmospheric concentration, ca. 380 ppm) at the initial time of sampling (to observe CO₂ bubbles it would be necessary to exceed this threshold). Similarly, the analyses of Casper et al. (2000) and Sepulveda-Jauregui et al. (2015) determined that only 1% of CO₂ was emitted by ebullition and 99% by diffusion in small shallow lakes. Together, our results may help to identify the environmental factors that regulate carbon emissions in small lakes. In freshwater systems, temperature controls the biological activity across food webs, the length of stratification periods and gas solubility. High temperatures amplified CH₄ emissions (Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018), which led to markedly higher amounts of CH₄ stored and emitted from the basins in the hotter summer of 2014 with a clear correlation between CH₄ emissions and temperature. Similar responses to regional temperature have been shown in ponds, in small shallow, and medium-sized lakes (Bartosiewicz, Laurion, & Macintyre, 2015; Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Liikanen, Huttunen, Valli, & Martikainen, 2002; Miettinen et al., 2015; Natchimuthu et al., 2014; Room et al., 2014) and in enclosure experiments (Audet et al., 2017; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017), suggesting that in predicted warming scenarios, an increase in carbon greenhouse gas emissions can be expected in lake ecosystems regardless of DOC inputs and their biogeochemical effects in the water column (e.g., in stratification, temperature regimes, pH, microbial metabolism and CO₂ dynamics). Despite the long-term division of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle that created two very different stable ecosystems with regard to carbon supply, the CH₄ and to some extent CO₂, emissions to the atmosphere were mainly determined by DOC-independent environmental conditions, as suggested by direct correlations between gas flux and temperature and between pH and dissolved gases. However, pH is an indirect factor associated with DOC correlation with dissolved gas concentrations. Therefore, the correlation between pH and dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ in the SW basin implied that DOC can play an important role in greenhouse gas emissions (Drake et al., 2018). In the case of CH₄, previous studies on methanogenesis in sediments of this acidic bog lake showed that the pathways to form CH₄ were similar to those in pH-neutral lakes (Conrad et al., 2010). Therefore, the reduction in DOC inputs to aquatic ecosystems would benefit several ecological and environmental issues, but in the context of CH₄ and CO₂ emission to the atmosphere from small lakes, the lake size and warming are probably the key factors for determining CH₄ and CO₂ emissions (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Kankaala, Huotari, Tulonen, & Ojala, 2013; Room et al., 2014; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2018; Yvon-Durocher et al., 2017). 4.2 | O₂ dynamics governing carbon greenhouse gas storage and emission Higher CH₄ emission periods coincided with the presence of extensive anoxic hypolimnia (in summer and fall). In contrast, low CH₄ emission periods were observed when the water column was oxygenated (in winter and early spring). We suggest that the presence of O₂ in the surficial sediment layers led to a decrease in methanogenic activity by inhibition because it is a strictly anaerobic process. Also, aerobic CH₄ oxidation likely occurred in the superficial sediment layers, further reducing the amount of CH₄ released to the water column. The reciprocal gradient between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ present during the stratification period suggested that CH₄ oxidation in the water column may have regulated diffusive CH₄ emission in stratification periods, but had little effect during mixing periods, as previously reported for lakes (Bartosiewicz et al., 2016; Casper et al., 2005; Encinas Fernández et al., 2014; Kankaala et al., 2006; Martinez-Cruz et al., 2015; Ricao Canelhas et al., 2016; Utsumi et al., 1998). The correlation analyses of dissolved gases (CH₄, CO₂ and O₂) showed that CH₄ and CO₂ are stored in anoxic layers and that they are indicators of high net heterotrophy (Borges et al., 2015; Sepulveda-Jauregui et al., 2015). The weaker correlation between CO₂ and O₂ (when compared to CH₄ and O₂) was consistent with previous reports of dissolved CO₂ patterns in acidic lakes (e.g., Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle) that are being strongly influenced by catchments rich in organic and inorganic carbon (Holgerson & Raymond, 2016; Tranvik et al., 2009; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). However, the reciprocal correlation between dissolved O₂ and CH₄ or CO₂ suggests that dissolved O₂ in the water column is an important indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ storage. Total carbon storage (calculated from dissolved CH₄ and CO₂ concentrations) followed dissolved O₂ changes over the seasons (Figure 7), with higher CH₄ and CO₂ emissions occurring when anoxic conditions predominated (maximum of 71 ± 13%, mean ± SD_y, pooled basins average). This may have been the result of higher microbial activity in the summer compared to colder periods of mixing; the reduction in the aerobic zone of the water column may have led to a decrease in aerobic methane oxidation activity. For more than 2 months during the winter, the water column was well oxygenated in both basins, and when temperature increased in spring, O₂ was quickly consumed in the newly established hypolimnia. Bartosiewicz et al. (2016) and Encinas Fernández et al. (2014) also found dissolved O₂ in the water column to be an indicator of CH₄ and CO₂ dynamics in summer. Moreover, Sabrekov et al. (2017) pointed out that O₂ patterns were among the major factors that controlled the dynamics of CH₄ and CO₂ in Siberian lakes, based on regional model development. Therefore, dissolved O₂ can be used as a tracer of biological activity associated with temperature and stratification changes during the seasons. Interestingly, we did not find any relationship between dissolved CH₄ or CO₂ and T or pH, when data from both basins were grouped. Instead, we found a positive correlation between pH and CO₂ and CH₄ concentrations when solely assessed in the water column of the SW basin. This correlation may indicate a higher microbial activity in all trophic levels (from primary production to heterotrophy) and not an intrinsic effect of recalcitrant DOC in the sediments (indicated by the low pH in the SW basin) on CH₄ and CO₂. Moreover, only the western basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle receive inflow from an adjacent peat bog (Burkert et al., 2004; Koschel, 1995), which may supply CH₄ and CO₂ and explain the positive correlation between pH and both gases. Such external sources have been suggested as an important source of both gases for freshwater ecosystems (Garcia-Tigreros Kodovska et al., 2016; Tank et al., 2018; Weyhenmeyer et al., 2015). FIGURE 7 Per cent of carbon stored (sum of CH₄–C and CO₂–C) in the anoxic (grey) and oxic (white) water layers in the water column during the time of the study in both basins of Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle beginning in August 2014 and ending in July 2015 5 | CONCLUDING REMARKS In the artificially divided Lake Grosse Fuchskuhle, the reduction in DOC inputs over 30 years to one of the studied basins was not the factor dominating CH4 and CO2 dynamics. Instead, seasonal changes in ambient temperature, O2 and stratification periods determined the relative contribution of cumulative carbon greenhouse gas emissions. Despite significant differences in pH and DOC developed between the two basins, CH4 and CO2 emissions were in the same order of magnitude over the year. The latter result shows the knowledge gap regarding the mineralisation processes of DOC in small acidic lakes. Therefore, the effect of DOC inputs to these types of lakes, including on CH4 and CO2 emissions, is still unclear. Further studies in various types of lakes are needed in order to better identify the effects of DOC on small and shallow lakes, which are a key component in global carbon greenhouse gas emissions. Biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment Chorng-Bin Hsu a, Hwey-Lian Hsieh b, Lei Yang c, Sheng-Hai Wu a, Jui-Sheng Chang d, Shu-Chuan Hsiao a, Hui-Chen Su e, Chao-Hsien Yeh e, Yi-Shen Ho f, Hsing-Juh Lin a,b,* a Department of Life Sciences, National Chung Hsing University, Taichung 40227, Taiwan b Biodiversity Research Center, Academia Sinica, Taipei 11529, Taiwan c Department of Marine Environment and Engineering, National Sun Yat-sen University, Kaohsiung 80424, Taiwan d Department of Leisure Management, Yu Da University, Miaoli 36143, Taiwan e Department of Water Resources Engineering and Conservation, Feng Chia University, Taichung 40724, Taiwan f Wild Bird Society of Taipei, Taipei 10664, Taiwan A R T I C L E I N F O Article history: Received 7 October 2010 Received in revised form 15 April 2011 Accepted 6 June 2011 Available online 2 July 2011 Keywords: Free-water-surface (FWS) constructed wetlands Subtropics Richness Diversity Community A B S T R A C T Constructed wetlands are often built for wastewater treatment to mitigate the adverse effects of organic pollution in streams and rivers caused by inputs of municipal wastewater. However, there has been little analysis of biodiversity and related factors influencing the ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the biodiversity of two free-water-surface integrated constructed wetlands in subtropical Taiwan by analyzing the water quality, habitat characteristics, and biotic communities of algae, macrophytes, birds, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the treatment cells. Our results indicated that the two integrated constructed wetlands (Hsin-Hai II and Daniaopi Constructed Wetlands) achieved good performance in reducing the concentrations of total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP), and loadings of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) from municipal sewage. In total, 58 bird species, 7 fish species, and 34 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were recorded in the two wetlands. The results of stepwise multiple regressions showed that the richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentrations. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Ordination analyses indicated that variations in the community structures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were respectively best explained by water temperature, wetland area, and species richness of fish. Our results suggest that wetland area, cover of aquatic macrophytes, and water quality were the most important factors governing the diversity in the constructed wetlands, and that the factors influencing community structures varied among different taxonomic groups. In addition to improving water quality, this study implied that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. © 2011 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Due to increasing population densities and impacts from human activities, pollution remains an essential issue for water quality protection and conservation of biodiversity in urban areas. There is a wide range of treatment technologies that can be used to improve the quality of wastewater to meet effluent standards. Many regions, however, do not have purification plants or lack sufficient capacity to treat all effluents due to the high costs of treatment processes (Kivaisi, 2002). The low coverage of sewage systems often results in municipal sewage and industrial wastewater being directly discharged into aquatic environments with no treatment (Jing et al., 2008). Wetlands are well known as one of the most productive ecosystems in the world (Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007). Countless species of birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians, fishes, and invertebrates depend on the water and vegetation in wetland habitats (Zedler and Kercher, 2005; Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Wetlands also directly and indirectly support people by providing ecosystem services such as flood abatement, food, a clean water supply, esthetic beauty, educational and recreational benefits, and carbon sinks (Zedler, 2003; Zedler and Kercher, 2005). The ability to simultaneously achieve water quality improvement and enhance biodiversity has generated increasing interest in constructing and restoring wetlands for wastewater treatment (Kivaisi, 2002). Constructed wetlands are artificial wetlands designed to intercept wastewater and remove a wide range of pollutants before discharge into natural water bodies. They mimic natural wetland ecosystems that combine physical, chemical, and biological processes to purify the water quality in more-controlled and efficient ways (Scholz et al., 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Constructed wetlands are widely used as low-cost alternatives to conventional tertiary municipal wastewater treatment worldwide (Kivaisi, 2002; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Researchers have demonstrated that constructed wetlands are effective for the onsite management of municipal and agricultural wastewater and can remove various nutrients, including suspended solids (SS), biological oxygen demand (BOD), chemical oxygen demand (COD), nitrogen, phosphorus, trace elements, and microorganisms contained in the wastewater (Rousseau et al., 2004; Mitsch and Gosselink, 2007; Scholz et al., 2007; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The success of constructed wetlands is frequently assessed based on the performance of pollution reduction (Rousseau et al., 2004; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). Constructed wetlands can also enhance various ecosystem services (Zedler and Kercher, 2005; Vymazal, 2011). Of the ecosystem services provided by wetlands, the biodiversity of constructed wetlands has attracted relatively less attention. Despite the rapid loss in wetland area and function (Zedler and Kercher, 2005), wetland biodiversity has been overlooked until recent decades (Denny, 1994). Wetland biodiversity is considered to have substantial conservation (Zedler and Kercher, 2005) and economic value (Costanza et al., 1997), and is also used as an indicator to assess ecosystem integrity (Mayer and Galatowitsch, 2001). Most studies addressing the biodiversity of constructed wetlands focused on a single taxonomic group (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000; Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Benyamine et al., 2004; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006; Jurado et al., 2010; Korfel et al., 2010). Although faunal diversity is thought to remain high in wetlands constructed for water treatment (Kadlec and Wallace, 2008), previous studies showed that high nutrient concentrations in wastewater are directly detrimental to wetland fauna (Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006) and to aquatic macrophyte communities, and, in turn, to the fauna that relies on macrophytes (Zhang et al., 2010). Although many studies have focused on the design of constructed wetlands to increase the pollutant removal efficiency (e.g., Thullen et al., 2005; Nahlil and Mitsch, 2006; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008), designing constructed wetlands it is more difficult to enhance biodiversity than to improve water quality, since there is a limited understanding of the factors that affect biodiversity (Zedler, 2003). There is an increasing trend to design multi-purpose treatment wetlands to enhance ancillary wildlife and human use benefits (Knight, 1992, 1997). An increasing number of studies have explored aquatic communities and factors influencing them in constructed wetlands (Fairchild et al., 2000; Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Balcombe et al., 2005; Canonico et al., 2005; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006; Jurado et al., 2010). However, the richness and diversity of different taxonomic groups in wetlands were determined by different factors in different regions (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Therefore, it is imperative for wetland managers to examine the relationship between environmental variables and biotic communities. Hansson et al. (2005) indicated the possibility of improving the design of wetlands in terms of both biodiversity and nutrient retention. The knowledge of relationships between environmental variables and biodiversity, especially in constructed wetlands, is of great value, not only because it is important in assessing ecosystem services provided by constructed wetlands, but also because it provides an essential tool for designing and managing wetlands in order to maintain and enhance biodiversity. In Taiwan, the water quality in many streams near urban areas is severely impacted by municipal wastewater, only <15% of which enters wastewater treatment plants (Jing et al., 2008). Under governmental support, constructed wetlands were widely built along riparian zones for on-site water treatment (Taiwan EPA, 2007). There are currently about 100 wetlands installed or under construction in Taiwan. Most of these constructed wetlands are located in riparian areas between levees and the river and are used to treat urban wastewater. Monitoring data show that these wetlands achieve an acceptable wastewater treatment performance (Jing et al., 2008). However, the biodiversity of these constructed wetlands is poorly understood. We investigated the effects of a number of environmental factors that may affect the diversity and community structures of wetland birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment. Understanding driving factors will be of benefit to managers involved in enhancing freshwater biodiversity on a large landscape scale. The objectives of this study were to (1) evaluate the biodiversity of different biotic communities, including aquatic macrophytes, birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates among treatment cells in two free-water-surface (FWS) integrated constructed wetlands along the riparian zone of the Da-Han River in subtropical Taiwan, (2) identify major factors influencing changes in the biodiversity of the constructed wetlands, and (3) examine relationships between the biotic community structure and environmental variables. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Study sites The Hsin-Hai II Constructed Wetland (HS2) and Daniaopi Constructed Wetland (DN) are five-cell FWS integrated wetlands, located in the riparian zone on the eastern bank of the Da-Han River in Taipei County (Fig. 1a). The HS2 and DN were respectively completed in September and November 2006. The DN covers a larger area with a higher flow rate and shorter hydraulic retention time than HS2 (Table 1). These two integrated wetlands have similar configurations, with each comprised of five treatment cells. The five sequential cells are a depositional pond, heavily vegetated pond I, open-water pond, heavily vegetated pond II, and ecological pond in the HS2 (cells HS2-1–HS2-5) (Fig. 1b and Table 2). The wastewater effluent from the ecological pond of HS2 flows directly into the Da-Han River after treatment. In the DN, the depositional pond (DN1) is followed by an open-water pond (DN2). The heavily vegetated pond I (DN3) is divided into four parallel sub-cells (DN3-A–DN3-D), each of which receives wastewater from the open-water pond and discharges outflow into the heavily vegetated pond II (DN4) and then into the ecological pond (DN5). After treatment, the wastewater effluent flows from the ecological pond (DN5) into a drainage channel and then into the Da-Han River (Fig. 1c and Table 2). We conducted water sampling and surveyed aquatic macrophytes and macroinvertebrates, fishes, and birds in the two constructed wetlands in February (winter) and June (summer) 2009, and bi-monthly from October 2009 to August 2010. Low-elevation aerial photos were also taken in February and June 2009 and January 2010. Fig. 1. (a) Locations and configurations of (b) the Hsin-Hai II Constructed Wetland (HS2) and (c) Daniaopi Constructed Wetland (DN). 2.2. Environmental variables The wetland area of each treatment cell was estimated based on aerial photographs using the software package, Image Pro 4.0 (Media Cybernetics, Silver Spring, MD). Water variables were measured in the field using portable instruments, such as water temperature (WTW LF196, Weilheim, Germany), dissolved oxygen (WTW oxi 3302), conductivity (WTW Cond 330i), and pH (WTW pH340). Water samples were taken from the outflow of each cell, immediately placed on ice in a cooler, and brought back to the laboratory for analyses of BOD, COD, nitrate (NO3⁻), nitrite (NO2⁻), total nitrogen (TN), total phosphorus (TP), suspended solids (SS), and phytoplankton chlorophyll (Chl)-a concentration following standard methods of the APHA (Clesceri et al., 1998). 2.3. Biotic samples Aquatic macrophytes were surveyed using transects across treatment cells. Six transects were set up in each treatment cell, and all aquatic macrophytes on the transects were identified to species level. To determine the cover of aquatic macrophytes, we overlaid a grid of 2.5-m plots onto an enlarged aerial photo of each treatment cell, and the cover of each species was determined by estimating the fractions of vegetation in each grid and summing up all grids. When areal photos were not available, the cover of aquatic macrophytes was estimated on each transect in the field. We used a D-net sweep (Model 7412D, BioQuip, Rancho Dominguez, CA) to collect aquatic invertebrates modified from a procedure of the USEPA (2002). During each sweep, the D-net was placed on the wetland bottom and pushed horizontally into the vegetation, if available, for a distance of 1 m to cover an area of about 0.3 m², while bouncing the net into the sediment at least twice. The distance between locations of adjacent sweeps was at least 1 m. Two sweeps were combined into one sample, and three samples (six sweeps) were taken in each treatment cell. brates were identified to the lowest possible taxonomic level and counted using a stereomicroscope in the laboratory. Nematodes and zooplankton taxa including cladoceran, copepods, and ostracods were excluded from further analyses. Major classes or orders were described for those specimens for which the species could not be determined. We used a cast net (2 m in radius with a 2-cm mesh size) and shrimp traps (15 cm in diameter) to collect fish from the constructed wetlands. The cast net was deployed three times in treatment cells where the method was applicable except in cells HS2-1, HS2-2, DN1, DN2, DN3-A, and DN3-D. Ten shrimp traps were also set up in each treatment cell. Caught fish were chilled on ice and transported back to the laboratory. A bird survey was conducted by three trained persons on three consecutive days, one for each constructed wetland. Observers patrolled the shores of treatment cells on foot during the first 3 h of daylight, and species and abundances in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands were determined with the aid of binoculars. The habitats where the birds were observed were also recorded. 2.4. Biotic metrics We assessed the biodiversity of constructed wetlands using two common measures of richness and the Shannon–Wiener index. Species richness (the number of species) was selected to represent the richness of birds, fishes, and aquatic macrophytes, whereas taxon richness (the number of taxa) was selected for aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands. The Shannon–Wiener index (\( H' \)) was calculated using the following equation: \[ H' = - \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i; \] where \( p_i \) is the proportion of individuals found of the ith species (taxon) or the percent coverage of the ith aquatic macrophyte species. 2.5. Statistical analysis Variables were first examined to see if they were normally distributed. DO, SS, BOD, COD, and NO\(_x^-\) (NO\(_2^-\) + NO\(_3^-\)) concentrations were log-transformed, while wetland areas and TN, TP, and phytoplankton Chl-a concentrations were square-root-transformed to improve the normality. Abundances of birds and fishes were square-root-transformed, and the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates was log(x + 1)-transformed. An arcsine-square-root transformation was used for the percent cover of aquatic macrophytes (Zar, 1996). We used multiple regressions to develop the most appropriate statistical models to predict biodiversity measures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the constructed wetlands. Species or taxon richness, abundance (density), and Shannon diversity (\( H' \)) of biotic communities were used as dependent variables, while wetland attributes, including wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics, were used as independent variables in a stepwise regression model (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Variables with a significance level of <0.05 were included in the regression models. We did not examine the diversity of aquatic macrophytes because most of the aquatic macrophyte species were artificially introduced when constructing the wetlands. Moreover, we used multivariate techniques to examine relationships of the community structures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates with environmental variables. The proportion of each species was separately calculated for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates. Rare species (taxa) were excluded from the analyses to reduce their influence on the ordinations (ter Braak, 1995). Only taxa constituting more than 0.5% of the total abundances for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were included in the multivariate analyses. Totals of 33 species of birds, 4 species of fishes, and 13 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were used in the analyses (Appendix A). A prior detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was separately conducted on the bird, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrate data to assess the gradient length of the first DCA axis. The lengths of the gradients were 3.957, 2.869, and 2.871 (in SD units) for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates, respectively. Therefore, the unimodal model (e.g., the canonical correspondence analysis, CCA) was more appropriate for birds, and a linear model (e.g., the redundancy analysis, RDA) was better for fishes and aquatic macroinvertebrates (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). In the ordination models, wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics were used as explanatory variables. We ran the analysis using the automatic forward-selection mode, and only variables explaining a significant proportion of the remaining variation were included (based on a Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations at \( p < 0.1 \)). Biodiversity measures were calculated using the PRIMER vers. 5 computer software (Clarke and Gorley, 2001). Multiple regression analyses were produced using the software package SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, 2003). Ordination analyses were performed using CANOCO for Windows vers. 4.52 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). 3. Results 3.1. Environmental variables Areas of treatment cells varied within and between constructed wetlands. The depositional ponds of the two constructed wetlands were small, at <0.2 ha. Areas of other treatment cells ranged 0.55–0.83 ha in the HS2 and 0.26–1.86 ha in the DN (Fig. 2). The cover of aquatic macrophytes was the highest in heavily vegetated ponds of each constructed wetland, i.e., HS2-2, HS2-4, DN3-A, DN3-B, and DN3-D (Fig. 2). Water quality widely varied among treatment cells in each constructed wetland. DO was low, generally <6 ppm except in the ecological ponds, and showed an increasing trend along the sequential treatment cells in both constructed wetlands (Table 2). In contrast, conductivity and concentrations of TN and TP showed a decreasing trend along sequential treatment cells, suggesting reductions in the pollutant concentrations of wastewater after passing through these constructed wetlands (Table 2). Other variables, however, fluctuated along the sequential treatment cells. The overall system performance of pollutant removal based on the reduction in concentrations in the water column is shown in Table 3. Removal of BOD and COD was higher in the HS2 with respective removal rates of 58.8% and 51.1%, and the outflow concentration was reduced to <11 and 30 mg L\(^{-1}\), respectively (Tables 2, 3). Concentrations of TN and TP were substantially reduced in the DN with respective removal rates of 51.4% and 52.3%, and the outflow concentrations were 8.4 and 0.5 ppm, respectively.

The average bird abundance and Shannon diversity (\( H' \)) were highest in the ecological ponds and lowest in the depositional ponds of both wetlands (Table 5). The dominant species was Chinese Bulbul (Pycnonotus sinensis), respectively accounting for 18.4% and 18.7% of the total abundances in the HS2 and DN. Only seven fish species were recorded in the two wetlands, and four of them, including tilapia (Oreochromis hybrid), topmouth gudgeon (Pseudorasbora parva), striped snakehead (Channa striata), and predatory carp (Erythrocultter erythropterus) are exotics. Levels of fish species richness were low in the two constructed wetlands with mean values ranging 0–1.6 in the HS2 and 1.0–2.4 in the DN (Table 5). Higher abundances and lower \( H' \) values were observed in treatment cells of the HS2 than in those of the DN (Table 5). The dominant species in the HS2 was blue gourami (Trichogaster trichopterus), which accounted for 91.3% of the total abundance. The DN was dominated by tilapia and goldfish (Carassius auratus auratus), accounting for 63.2% and 35.0% of the total abundance, respectively. The mean taxon richness of aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell ranged 7.1–10.8 in the HS2 and 7.3–15.0 in the DN (Table 5). In the HS2, densities of aquatic macroinvertebrates were higher in HS2-2 and HS2-3 with mean values of 210.0 and 248.2 individuals m\(^{-2}\), respectively. Densities in the DN were higher in DN2 and DN1 followed by DN3-B and DN3-A (Table 5). Mean \( H' \) of aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell was similar, ranging 1.20–1.73 in the HS2 and 0.85–1.67 in the DN. The dominant taxa in the HS2 were mosquitoes (Culex spp.) and non-biting midges (Chironomidae), which respectively accounted for 33.4% and 13.6% of the total abundance. The DN was dominated by oligochaetes and chironomids, which respectively accounted for 59.0% and 8.0% of the total abundance. 3.3. Factors affecting biotic metrics in the constructed wetlands Results from stepwise multiple regressions showed that the biodiversity and abundance of different taxonomic groups were affected by different environmental variables (Table 6). Species richness, abundance, and \( H' \) of wetland birds were positively related to the wetland area, while \( H' \) was also correlated with the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Table 6). Species richness of fishes was positively related to the wetland area and negatively related to conductivity and \( H' \) of aquatic macrophytes. Fish abundance was positively related to DO, while \( H' \) was negatively related to the TP concentration (Table 6). For aquatic macroinvertebrates, taxon richness and density were positively correlated with the cover of aquatic macrophytes and negatively with COD. \( H' \) of aquatic macroinvertebrates was positively related to the wetland area, although the \( R^2 \) value was low (Table 6). Species richness, abundance, and \( H' \) of wetland birds increased with wetland area up to about 2 ha (Fig. 3). Species richness of fishes and the taxon richness of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes, respectively. However, relations between environmental variables and other biotic metrics of fish and aquatic macroinvertebrates were not clear. 3.4. The RDA ordination plot indicated that narrow-winged damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Diplonychus sp.) and leaf beetle larvae (Chrysomelidae) were more abundant in treatment cells with high cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Dipteran species such as mosquitoes (Culex spp.), brine flies (Ephydridae), and non-biting midges (Chironomidae) were more abundant in treatment cells with high values of conductivity and low values of DO (Fig. 6). 4. Discussion 4.1. Performance of pollutant removal The construction of wetlands is an alternative measure to conventional water treatment, which provides a potentially more environmentally friendly and economical treatment system to mitigate the negative effects of domestic wastewater and urban runoff (Scholz et al., 2007). Our study showed that the two constructed wetlands were effective in nutrient removal, although the performances varied between the constructed wetlands and also among nutrients. Wetland design, water quality, hydraulics, soil chem- istry, microbial communities, macroinvertebrates, and vegetation each may greatly affect the performance of constructed wetlands. The main removal mechanisms of BOD and COD include microbial degradation and settling of colloidal particles (Vymazal et al., 1998). Nitrogen is primarily removed through microbial nitrification and denitrification in most constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998). Phosphorus removal in constructed wetlands occurs from absorption and precipitation by soil particles (Vymazal, 2010). The amount of nutrients such as phosphorus removed by plant uptake generally accounts for a small fraction of total nutrients removed in constructed wetlands (Vymazal et al., 1998), and may be released back into the water after plants decay (Vymazal, 2010). Small and deep wetlands increase phosphorus retention by increasing particle sedimentation, while large surface areas may maximize nitrogen removal (Hansson et al., 2005; Kadlec and Wallace, 2008). The removal rates in this study were similar compared to nearby constructed wetlands (Fan et al., 2009). 4.2. Biodiversity of constructed wetlands Along with treating wastewater, there is an increasing trend in designing constructed wetlands to restore degraded habitats for wildlife. However, different ecological functions of wetland systems are thought to be conflicting. High nutrient loadings that surpass a critical level may cause dramatic shifts in species composition and ecosystem functioning (Verhoeven et al., 2006). Some potential problems, including bioaccumulation of toxic materials, transmission of disease, and environmental hazards, might result from the use of wetlands for wastewater treatment (Knight, 1992). Benyamine et al. (2004) indicated that the typical single-objective focus of scientific studies has led to contradictions in recommendations for the design and management of constructed wetlands for multiple uses. Nevertheless, this study combined with others (e.g., Knight, 1997; Fleming-Singer and Horne, 2006) suggest that constructed wetlands can provide attractive habitats for various kinds of wildlife. Meanwhile, after reviewing the North American Treatment Wetland (NADB) Database, Knight et al. (2001) indicated that there were no detrimental effects on wildlife caused by the pollution-cleansing function of treatment wetlands. Due to a lack of data in nearby freshwater habitats, the contribution of constructed wetlands to landscape biodiversity could not be determined in this study. Nevertheless, in addition to water quality improvement, this study suggests that the biodiversity of constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment can be enhanced through proper design and management. This study further demonstrated that the biodiversity of different taxonomic groups in constructed wetlands is governed by various factors. 4.3. Factors affecting wetland biodiversity Our results suggest a positive relationship between the area of a constructed wetland and the biodiversity and abundance of birds, which is in accordance with other studies on wetlands (Zedler, 2003; Hansson et al., 2005). In addition to wetland area, bird biodiversity was found to be affected by adjacent and regional land uses, such as road density and connectedness (Whited et al., 2000). Ordination results suggested that bird communities were mainly determined by seasonal patterns, as well as food availability and nesting requirements for brood rearing. Bird species such as the Dusky Thrush, Teal, and Yellow Wagtail were winter visitors (Shiu et al., 2005), and, therefore, were negatively correlated with water temperature. Members of the Ardeidae such as Little Egrets and Black-crowned Night Herons, and the Recurvirostridae like Black-winged Stilts were found to be associated with the species richness and abundance of fishes (Fig. 4). A number of studies indicated that they feed on a wide variety of prey types but mainly on fish (Fasola, 1994; Kazantzidis and Goutner, 2005). The association of White-breasted Waterhen (Amaurornis phoenicurus) with aquatic macrophytes can be attributed to nest-site selection for brood rearing (Gopakumar and Kaimal, 2008). Aquatic invertebrates are primary food resources for many wintering waterbirds. Wallau et al. (2010) indicated that the Common Moorhen feeds on pieces of aquatic macrophytes and removes macrophytes to search for invertebrates which utilize macrophytes as habitats. The Cattle Egret was found to rely heavily on various invertebrates as their main food sources (Lombardini et al., 2001), and its number was positively correlated with the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates (Fig. 4). Teal and Spot-billed Duck (Anatidae) may also compete with fish for the same food resources (invertebrates) and are thus found in lower densities at wetlands with fish compared to those without fish (e.g., Eriksson, 1979). Our study showed that fish biodiversity was low in these young (<5 years) constructed wetlands. Hansson et al. (2005) also found similar results and indicated that natural wetlands aged more than 100 years showed considerably higher fish species richness than young constructed wetlands. In constructed wetlands, possible sources of the fish are limited to those from nearby streams during floods and mercy releases, and, therefore, the biodiversity of fish is unlikely to increase over a short time period. This study showed that a wetland’s area is also important in determining the species richness of fishes. All treatment cells in our study were <2 ha (Fig. 2). Søndergaard et al. (2005) found that fish species richness was low, typically 1–3 species, in Danish ponds and lakes with areas of <1 ha, and gradually increased with lake size. Scheffer et al. (2006) proposed that fish are rare in small, isolated lakes, probably as a result of a higher likelihood of fish kills combined with their low colonizing ability. Moreover, fish biodiversity appeared to be most affected by the water quality in constructed wetlands. Fish species found in constructed wetlands appeared to be tolerant of high nutrient levels and low DO conditions. Blue gourami is an obligate air-breathing fish (Burggren, 1979), which means that it can adapt to changing DO levels in constructed wetlands. The dominant blue gourami and tilapia in constructed wetlands are exotics, but not the goldfish. Tilapia (Cichlidae) are among the most widely distributed exotic fishes in the world (Canonico et al., 2005). Studies found that they are able to respond to environmental changes by rapidly altering their life history characteristic and trophic levels (Bowen and Allanson, 1982), which may benefit their invasion into new environments (Holway and Suarez, 1999). The exotic species introduced to these wetlands either on purpose or accidentally may also threaten populations of native species. Our results suggest close relationships of the richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates with the coverage of aquatic macrophytes. The abundance and diversity of aquatic invertebrates were found to be associated with the vegetated area of wetlands (Gee et al., 1997). The presence of aquatic macrophytes might affect the distributions of aquatic macroinvertebrates and thus their biodiversity in several ways. Submerged vegetation in aquatic ecosystems forms complex structures, which may be used as habitats (Gee et al., 1997) or as refuges to reduce the foraging efficiency of predators (Diehl, 1992). Because there is more space for food attachment and collection, aquatic macrophytes provide additional resources such as epiphytes to the macroinvertebrate community, especially for grazers and thus may indirectly favor detritivores and predators (Diehl, 1992). Positive relationships between the abundance of aquatic macroinvertebrates and cover of aquatic macrophytes were reported elsewhere (de Szalay and Resh, 2000). In constructed wetlands, excessive nutrient loadings, high toxic pollutant levels, and anaerobic conditions often prevent aquatic macroinvertebrates from using wetlands as habitats (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Verhoeven et al., 2006). Hence, our results indicated a negative relationship of COD with the taxon richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates. Decreases in richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates were shown to be related to changes in water quality in various aquatic ecosystems (e.g., Spieles and Mitsch, 2000; Jurado et al., 2010). The community structure of aquatic macroinvertebrates in constructed wetlands was influenced by the presence of predators and suitable habitats. Fish are often the top predators in wetland ecosystems and can impact aquatic macroinvertebrates in terms of species richness, density, diversity, and community structure (Diehl, 1992). Ordination analyses indicated that the major dipteran taxa in these constructed wetlands, such as non-biting midges (Chironomidae), mosquitoes (Culicidae), and brine flies (Ephydridae), were negatively associated with the species richness of fish and dissolved oxygen. Most of the fish species in our study sites rely on aquatic invertebrates as their main food sources. The diet of the blue gourami mainly consists of aquatic invertebrates and algae-based foods (Syarifuddin and Kramer, 1996). Although goldfish predominantly eat non-animal food, studies showed that they also feed on a wide range of food resources, including various zooplankton and aquatic insects (e.g., Peterson et al., 2005). Numerous studies demonstrated that the presence of fish may reduce the density and biomass of certain taxa of aquatic invertebrates (e.g., Fairchild et al., 2000) and change the community structure of aquatic invertebrates in wetlands (Tarr et al., 2005). Moreover, many species of these dipteran families are tolerant of low DO and polluted water (Courtney et al., 1996). Relationships of damselflies (Coenagrionidae), giant water bugs (Belostomatidae), and leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae) with the cover of aquatic macrophytes suggest that the vegetation is used as food and perch sites (Cloarec, 1990; Gibbons et al., 2002; Fernandez and Hilker, 2007). The amount of unexplained variation in our models suggests that some other unmeasured variables play certain roles in regulating communities in these constructed wetlands. Keddy and Fraser (2000) suggested that variations in water depth were the most important factor governing communities in shoreline wetlands. Increases in habitat heterogeneity or complexity (Hansson et al., 2005) and age (Fairchild et al., 2000) may increase the biodiversity of wetlands. In addition, the richness of aquatic invertebrates increases with the hydroperiod, i.e., the length of time that a wetland holds water (Tarr et al., 2005). In highly connected wetlands, aquatic invertebrate richness may also increase through dispersal from areas with different environmental conditions (e.g., Cottenie and De Meester, 2003). These factors could be constructed and manipulated through proper design and management of constructed wetlands, and can therefore be used to increase biodiversity. 4.4. Implications for the design and management of constructed wetlands Previous studies examined the impacts of environmental factors on biodiversity across various taxonomic groups in lentic ecosystems (e.g., Findlay and Houlahan, 1997; Balcombe et al., 2005; Declerck et al., 2005; Hansson et al., 2005). Results from those studies as well as ours reveal that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. In order to maximize biodiversity in constructed wetlands, the factors involved in each taxonomic group should be taken into consideration in wetland design and management from a holistic view. According to our results, wetland area and cover of aquatic macrophytes appeared to be the two most important factors affecting biodiversity in the constructed wetlands. A wetland constructed with the aim of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Findlay and Houlahan (1997) found that species richness of all taxa in their study, including birds, mammals, herptiles and plants, increased with wetland area. Whatever other considerations may be taken into the wetland design, from a biodiversity conservation perspective, bigger is indeed better, although the maximum richness of some taxa might be encountered at a certain area (e.g., 4–5 ha for birds, Hansson et al., 2005). Changes in macrophyte composition and cover are among the most important ecological successions in constructed wetlands (Mitsch et al., 2005). Although high macrophyte cover may increase taxa richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates, problems can arise as a result of the presence of dense vegetation in wetlands such as consumption of DO and contribution to nutrient loadings as plants decompose (Sartoris et al., 2000). For wastewater treatment, a high cover of aquatic macrophytes was designed as one of the important factors facilitating N retention (Thiere et al., 2011). For wildlife management, a 50:50 ratio of open water to emergent vegetation, i.e., hemi-marshes, was recommended to attract wildlife (Murkin et al., 1997). de Szalay and Resh (2000) indicated that the cover of aquatic macrophytes increased the abundances of some dipteran taxa, which might cause serious nuisance problems in wetlands. Our results also show that taxa responded differently to changes in the cover of aquatic macrophytes (Fig. 6). Since the vegetation has both positive and negative effects on the performance of constructed wetland for wastewater treatment, a proper vegetation balance is needed for optimal treatment performance through vegetation management (Thullen et al., 2005). It is widely accepted that created wetlands, whether for wastewater treatment or not, may never express the full range of ecological variability found in natural wetlands (Brooks et al., 2005). However, as water quality improves due to sequential purification along the treatment cells, the last ponds in a constructed wetland may be capable of supporting biodiversity similar to that of natural wetlands (Jurado et al., 2010). 5. Conclusions Although characterized by high nutrient loadings, constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment are able to support various wildlife and enhance biodiversity. This study indicated that the factors influencing biodiversity differed among faunal groups in constructed wetlands. The richness, abundance, and diversity of birds increased with the wetland area. Fish richness and abundance respectively increased with wetland area and dissolved oxygen, while the diversity decreased with increases in TP concentration. The richness and density of aquatic macroinvertebrates increased with the cover of aquatic macrophytes, while the diversity increased with wetland area. Therefore, a wetland constructed with the aims of improving water quality and enhancing biodiversity should have a large surface area and a high cover of aquatic macrophytes. Our results imply that ecosystem functioning of constructed wetlands, used primarily for wastewater treatment or created for new wetland areas, can be managed to enhance biodiversity. Nematodes and zooplankton taxa including cladoceran, copepods, and ostracods were excluded from further analyses. Major classes or orders were described for those specimens for which the species could not be determined. We used a cast net (2 m in radius with a 2-cm mesh size) and shrimp traps (15 cm in diameter) to collect fish from the constructed wetlands. The cast net was deployed three times in treatment cells where the method was applicable except in cells HS2-1, HS2-2, DN1, DN2, DN3-A, and DN3-D. Ten shrimp traps were also set up in each treatment cell. Caught fish were chilled on ice and transported back to the laboratory. A bird survey was conducted by three trained persons on three consecutive days, one for each constructed wetland. Observers patrolled the shores of treatment cells on foot during the first 3 h of daylight, and species and abundances in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands were determined with the aid of binoculars. The habitats where the birds were observed were also recorded. 2.4. Biotic metrics We assessed the biodiversity of constructed wetlands using two common measures of richness and the Shannon–Wiener index. Species richness (the number of species) was selected to represent the richness of birds, fishes, and aquatic macrophytes, whereas taxon richness (the number of taxa) was selected for aquatic macroinvertebrates in each treatment cell of the two constructed wetlands. The Shannon–Wiener index (\( H' \)) was calculated using the following equation: \[ H' = - \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i; \] where \( p_i \) is the proportion of individuals found of the ith species (taxon) or the percent coverage of the ith aquatic macrophyte species. 2.5. Statistical analysis Variables were first examined to see if they were normally distributed. DO, SS, BOD, COD, and NO\(_x^-\) (NO\(_2^-\) + NO\(_3^-\)) concentrations were log-transformed, while wetland areas and TN, TP, and phytoplankton Chl-a concentrations were square-root-transformed to improve the normality. Abundances of birds and fishes were square-root-transformed, and the density of aquatic macroinvertebrates was log(x + 1)-transformed. An arcsine-square-root transformation was used for the percent cover of aquatic macrophytes (Zar, 1996). We used multiple regressions to develop the most appropriate statistical models to predict biodiversity measures of birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates in the constructed wetlands. Species or taxon richness, abundance (density), and Shannon diversity (\( H' \)) of biotic communities were used as dependent variables, while wetland attributes, including wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics, were used as independent variables in a stepwise regression model (Sokal and Rohlf, 1995). Variables with a significance level of <0.05 were included in the regression models. We did not examine the diversity of aquatic macrophytes because most of the aquatic macrophyte species were artificially introduced when constructing the wetlands. Moreover, we used multivariate techniques to examine relationships of the community structures of birds, fishes, and aquatic
pages.4:
macroinvertebrates with environmental variables. The proportion of each species was separately calculated for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates. Rare species (taxa) were excluded from the analyses to reduce their influence on the ordinations (ter Braak, 1995). Only taxa constituting more than 0.5% of the total abundances for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates were included in the multivariate analyses. Totals of 33 species of birds, 4 species of fishes, and 13 aquatic macroinvertebrate taxa were used in the analyses (Appendix A). A prior detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) was separately conducted on the bird, fish, and aquatic macroinvertebrate data to assess the gradient length of the first DCA axis. The lengths of the gradients were 3.957, 2.869, and 2.871 (in SD units) for birds, fishes, and aquatic macroinvertebrates, respectively. Therefore, the unimodal model (e.g., the canonical correspondence analysis, CCA) was more appropriate for birds, and a linear model (e.g., the redundancy analysis, RDA) was better for fishes and aquatic macroinvertebrates (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). In the ordination models, wetland area, water quality, and biotic metrics were used as explanatory variables. We ran the analysis using the automatic forward-selection mode, and only variables explaining a significant proportion of the remaining variation were included (based on a Monte Carlo test with 999 permutations at \( p < 0.1 \)). Biodiversity measures were calculated using the PRIMER vers. 5 computer software (Clarke and Gorley, 2001). Multiple regression analyses were produced using the software package SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, 2003). Ordination analyses were performed using CANOCO for Windows vers. 4.52 (ter Braak and Šmilauer, 2002). 3. Results 3.1. Environmental variables Areas of treatment cells varied within and between constructed wetlands. The depositional ponds of the two constructed wetlands were small, at <0.2 ha. Areas of other treatment cells ranged 0.55–0.83 ha in the HS2 and 0.26–1.86 ha in the DN (Fig. 2). The cover of aquatic macrophytes was the highest in heavily vegetated ponds of each constructed wetland, i.e., HS2-2, HS2-4, DN3-A, DN3-B, and DN3-D (Fig. 2). Water quality widely varied among treatment cells in each constructed wetland. DO was low, generally <6 ppm except in the ecological ponds, and showed an increasing trend along the sequential treatment cells in both constructed wetlands (Table 2). In contrast, conductivity and concentrations of TN and TP showed a decreasing trend along sequential treatment cells, suggesting reductions in the pollutant concentrations of wastewater after passing through these constructed wetlands (Table 2). Other variables, however, fluctuated along the sequential treatment cells. The overall system performance of pollutant removal based on the reduction in concentrations in the water column is shown in Table 3. Removal of BOD and COD was higher in the HS2 with respective removal rates of 58.8% and 51.1%, and the outflow concentration was reduced to <11 and 30 mg L\(^{-1}\), respectively (Tables 2, 3). Concentrations of TN and TP were substantially reduced in the DN with respective removal rates of 51.4% and 52.3%, and the outflow concentrations were 8.4 and 0.5 ppm, respectively.

Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison E. Einola,1 M. Rantakari,2 P. Kankaala,3 P. Kortelainen,2 A. Ojala,4 H. Pajunen,5 S. Mäkelä,1 and L. Arvola1 Received 23 December 2010; revised 6 May 2011; accepted 18 May 2011; published 27 July 2011. [1] Lakes play an important role in catchment carbon (C) balances. However, the role of lakes in landscape C cycling in changing climate is highly uncertain. We studied C pools in a chain of five boreal lakes and compared the C fluxes during a wet and a dry year. The included pools were dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) and total organic carbon (TOC) in lake water, as well as C pools in littoral macrophytes and lake sediments. The estimated C fluxes consisted of hydrological input and output of DIC and TOC, emission of carbon dioxide (CO2) to the atmosphere, DIC incorporated as organic carbon in primary production of phytoplankton and littoral macrophytes, and sedimentation of C. The riverine input of C into the lakes increased remarkably (40–210%) in the year with high precipitation. Simultaneously, there was a clear increase in the flux of CO2 to the atmosphere from the three small uppermost lakes, whereas in two large lowland lakes the CO2 fluxes were higher during the warm dry year. On the landscape scale, the role of small lakes (area <1 km2) was emphasized in net C accumulation, whereas the large lowland lakes released more CO2 to the atmosphere. In parallel, the concentration of TOC in the water column decreased downstream the lake chain whereas DIC increased. The largest pool of C (>98%) in all the lakes was in the sediment. Sediment C store, calculated relative to the lake area, was positively correlated with lake water TOC (r2 = 0.93, P < 0.05) and Fe (r2 = 0.96, P < 0.05) concentrations. Lake water Fe content was also a good predictor for the long-term accumulation (r2 = 0.99, P < 0.01), as well as gross sedimentation rate of organic carbon (r2 = 0.48, P < 0.01). Citation: Einola, E., M. Rantakari, P. Kankaala, P. Kortelainen, A. Ojala, H. Pajunen, S. Mäkelä, and L. Arvola (2011), Carbon pools and fluxes in a chain of five boreal lakes: A dry and wet year comparison, J. Geophys. Res., 116, G03009, doi:10.1029/2010JG001636. 1. Introduction [2] Although freshwater lakes and rivers cover a small area of the earth’s surface, their role in regional carbon (C) budgets and also in global C cycling is much more pronounced than expected only by their area. Rivers and lakes transport, mineralize and accumulate significant amounts of terrestrially fixed C and exchange inorganic C between water-air interfaces [e.g., del Giorgio and Peters, 1994; Kortelainen et al., 2004; Cole et al., 2007; Downing, 2010]. [3] The riverine transport of organic carbon plays an important role in functioning of boreal lakes; e.g., in humic lakes, common in the Boreal Zone, terrestrial carbon input can be much higher than in-lake production [Sarvala et al., 1981; Arvola et al., 1990; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the majority of lakes and rivers are net heterotrophic, i.e., the biological C mineralization exceeds primary production [Alin and Johnson, 2007; Tranvik et al., 2009]. Moreover, the recent trend of increasing concentrations of colored organic substances in many northern lakes and rivers [e.g., Monteith et al., 2007; Lepistö et al., 2008] may further strengthen heterotrophy in these freshwater ecosystems because of decreasing light availability for primary producers. [4] In the Boreal Zone, the concentration of total organic carbon (TOC) in lakes and the export of TOC from catchments are strongly related to the coverage of peatlands [Kortelainen, 1993; Kortelainen et al., 2006a] and coniferous forests in the catchment area [Mattsson et al., 2003; Humborg et al., 2004]. Most (>80%) of the organic matter exported from the catchments is in dissolved form [Wetzel, 2001]. A small proportion of the dissolved organic matter (DOM) may aggregate with metals (amorphous iron and aluminum) [Jonsson, 1997] and/or flocculate with bacteria [von Wachenfeldt et al., 2009], contributing to C accumulation in bottom sediments. In small boreal headwater streams as well as large rivers flowing to the Figure 1. Map of the study area showing the study lakes, the rivers connecting them, and the vegetation type and land use of each study lake. Thick arrows indicate the main inlets of rivers running to and from the study lakes. Baltic Sea, the proportion of particulate organic carbon (POC) of TOC is <5% [Kortelainen et al., 2006a; Mattsson et al., 2005]. The contribution of living material is low especially in running waters, where bacteria, algae, protozoa and larger zooplankton may comprise only about 1% of the TOC [Arvola and Nurmesniemi, 2000]. [5] Most lakes in the Boreal Zone are connected by streams as chains that can differ considerably in their morphology and physical and chemical characteristics. The residence time of water in each basin, defined by the catchment setting and lake morphology, together with the average annual runoff, may be crucial for biogeochemical processing of the organic matter [cf. Algesten et al., 2004], i.e., for microbial decomposition in the water column and in the sediment as well as ultraviolet (UV) irradiance-induced breakdown in the uppermost water layer [Vähätalo et al., 2000; Jonsson et al., 2001]. As a consequence, the residence time influences the quantity and quality of organic matter flowing downstream, and the proportion of organic C released as carbon dioxide (CO_2) and methane (CH_4), or stored in the bottom sediments. Mattsson et al. [2005] showed that proportion of lake area in the upper catchment significantly reduced TOC transport by the large Finnish rivers to the coast. Thus, upstream lakes may be intensive sites for DOM processing, which decreases the export of C downstream [Rasmussen et al., 1989; Kortelainen, 1993; Larson et al., 2007]. [6] Climate change scenarios predict increasing precipitation and temperature for many areas in the Boreal Zone, resulting in major changes in seasonal runoff patterns in northern catchments [e.g., Andréasson et al., 2004], including increasing frequency of extreme weather conditions and thus also extremes in hydrology [e.g., Christensen and Christensen, 2003]. Since hydrology is a major driver of the variability of water C concentrations on the catchment scale [e.g., Erlandsson et al., 2008], the interannual variations in C budgets of individual lakes may be considerable [Arvola et al., 1990]. Although carbon budgets for single lakes [e.g., Arvola et al., 1990; Sobek et al., 2006] and also for a chain of hard-water lakes [Finlay et al., 2010] have been studied, C budgets for a chain of boreal lakes in climatically different years have remained unknown. [7] The aim of our study was to (1) estimate C pools (store in the sediment and in the water column and biomass of primary producers) in a chain of five boreal lakes consisting of one small headwater lake, two small drainage lakes, and two large downstream lakes and to (2) compare C fluxes (net primary production, inflow, outflow, sedimentation, and atmospheric efflux) between a dry and a rainy year within this Table 1. Material and Methods [8] The five study lakes (areal range 0.036–44 km2), situated in the southern Boreal Zone in Finland were numbered by their order in the chain: (1) Valkea-Kotinen, (2) Alinen Rautjärvi, (3) Ekojärvi, (4) Kuohijärvi, and (5) Kukkia (Figure 1). The area deglaciated about 11,500 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. The uppermost and the smallest lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), was isolated immediately after deglaciation, while the other lakes were submerged by waters of the ancient Baltic Sea. Since the postglacial land uplift was more rapid than the rise of sea level, the land area expanded and new lakes became isolated. Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) was isolated about 11,400 years ago, Lake Ekojärvi (3) about 9800 years ago and the largest lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) about 9700 years ago [Pajunen, 2004]. [9] The Precambrian bedrock in the area consists of veined gneiss with granodiorite occurring around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and close to Lake Kuohijärvi (4). The soil is mostly moraine but there is gravel and sand around Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and the river draining it, while clay areas partly surround lakes Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5). Coniferous forests with Norway Spruce (Picea abies [L.] H. Karst.) and Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris L.) cover 65–80% and peatlands less than 20% of the catchment areas of each lake (Figure 1). Except for the first lake of the chain, Valkea-Kotinen, which is situated in a nature reserve area, the human impact on the catchments has been quite intense, because of a >150 year long history of forestry and related activities, including draining of wetlands. Some agriculture is also practiced, predominantly in the lowland areas, but the proportion of agricultural land in the catchment does not exceed 5% around any of the studied lakes. The local names suggest that historically the local people have utilized lake iron (e.g., Alinen Rautjärvi = Lower Iron Lake). The lakes vary in their morphological characteristics (Table 1), and the lake area to catchment area ratio (LA/CA) is significantly higher in the two largest lowland lakes than in the first three lakes in the chain. The concentrations of TOC, total phosphorus, total nitrogen and chlorophyll \( a \) are higher in the small upstream lakes than in the largest lowland lakes (Table 2). In the uppermost lake, Valkea-Kotinen (1), the hypolimnion is anoxic during winter and summer stratification. In Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Ekojärvi (3), the hypolimnetic anoxia during the stratification periods is occasional, whereas in Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5) the entire water column is oxic throughout the year. The larger lakes are covered by ice usually from late November to late April and the smaller ones from late October or early November to early May. [10] The annual long-term (1987–2007) average precipitation in the area is 632 mm (Finnish Meteorological Institute). The highest runoff peaks are generally observed in spring after snowmelt. The runoff can also peak during autumn, when precipitation is generally higher than in summer and the evapotranspiration is small. However, high runoffs can also occur during summer, as in 1998, if the precipitation is high and the antecedent soil conditions are wet. [11] The annual precipitation during 1997 was 5% lower and during 1998 22% higher than the average (Table 3), with the most distinguishable difference in the precipitation patterns observed in summer: in 1997 the summer precipitation was 10% lower than the long-term average, while in 1998 it was 70% higher than the average. The differences in precipitation were reflected in the water residence time of the lakes. There was also a difference of almost 2°C between the daily average air temperatures during the two summers (Table 3). For the fifth lake in the chain (Kukkia) the data set was not sufficient for budget calculations. [13] In the three small uppermost lakes the sediment volume was estimated on the basis of coring and survey on site. The interface between organic sediment (gyttja, clay gyttja or gyttja clay) and the underlying mineral soil (till, sand, silt or clay) was interpreted to indicate lake isolation. The thickness of the lake sediment bed was determined at seven sites in Lake Valkea-Kotinen (1), 35 sites in Lake Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and 48 sites in Lake Ekojärvi (3). In the largest lowland lakes, Kuohijärvi (4) and Kukkia (5), echo sounding was used to estimate the volume of the lake sediment bed with survey transects of 15 and 31 km, respectively. In these transects the proportion of accumulation bottom was measured. This proportion and the total lake area were used to estimate the accumulation area, which was multiplied with the average thickness to obtain the sediment volume. For the analysis of sediment density and C content, a sediment core was collected from each lake. The cores extended from the surface of the sediment bed to the depth of lake isolation. In the laboratory the cores were opened and their stratigraphy determined. The cores were divided into samples and a total of 104 samples were analyzed. The sample treatment and laboratory methods are thoroughly described by Pajunen et al. [2000]. The amount of total dry matter is based on sediment volume and average density and the amount of C on the amount of total dry matter and average C content. The average C store (g C m⁻²) was divided by the age of the lake to obtain the average Holocene accumulation rates (g C m⁻² yr⁻¹). [14] The gross sedimentation rate was measured only in the uppermost lake as part of a long-term monitoring program [cf. Keskitalo and Salonen, 1994]. Sedimenting material was collected with three acrylic plastic tubes (length 45 cm, diameter 5 cm) placed below the epilimnion at a depth of 4 m. During the ice-free period, material settled in the tubes was removed every 2 weeks, dried, weighed and analyzed for C content with a high-temperature combustion method [Salonen, 1979]. For annual estimates of gross sedimentation we used the results from the under ice measurements, conducted in 1995 and 1996 with exactly the same methods as during the open water period but using a 3 week collection period. In addition to C, the Fe content of the gross sedimentation was measured during one open water season (in 2000) with a Varian AAS (Varian Inc. Palo Alto, Calif., United States). [15] The samples for TOC and DIC analyses of the water column were taken at 0.2–05 m depth in rivers and at 1 m depth in the lakes. The sampling frequency in the rivers was primarily once a month during the open water season (May–November) and once in winter (early April). The uppermost lake (Valkea-Kotinen) was sampled 24 times during the both years. The other lakes in the chain were sampled 1–4 times in 1997 and four times in 1998 (late winter, spring, summer, and autumnal mixing). For the missing data for spring 1997 in Alinen Rautjärvi (2) and Kukkia (5), and for winter, spring and autumn 1997 in Kuohijärvi (4) the values for the corresponding season of 1998 were used. [16] The TOC concentration of the water was analyzed with a Shimadzu TOC-500 analyzer (Shimadzu Corp. Kyoto, Japan). For some occasions (about half of the river samples), water color values (platinum reference) were available instead of TOC. However, TOC was linearly related to water color in the samples taken from the study rivers and the lakes, and the missing TOC values were estimated with the regression equation: TOC [mg C L⁻¹] = 0.0408 * water color [mg Pt L⁻¹] + 5.29 (r² = 0.84, P < 0.05, n = 110). The DIC concentrations were estimated from the measured alkalinity values with the regression equation DIC [μmol L⁻¹] = 0.996 * Alkalinity [μeq L⁻¹] + 19.3, r² = 0.95, n = 874, obtained from measurements in randomly selected Finnish soft water lakes with similar range of alkalinity [Rantakari and Kortelainen, 2008]. Temperature and oxygen concentration in the water column of the lakes was measured with YSI 55 (Yellow Springs Instruments) combined probe (accuracy ±0.3°C, ±0.3 mg O₂ L⁻¹). [17] The discharge from each subcatchment was estimated using measured daily runoff data for the years 1997 and 1998 (Finnish Environment Institute, OIVA service on environment and geographic information, 17 March 2010) from the rivers Mustajoki and Haarajoki, both situated less than 30 km from the study sites and having land use characteristics very similar to the study lakes, assuming that the discharge from each subcatchment was related to its area. The TOC and DIC input and output were calculated by multiplying the monthly discharge (the sum of measured daily values) at the inflows and outflows with the TOC and DIC concentration during the respective period in the rivers between the lakes. The min-max range of the annual TOC and DIC loads to lakes were estimated by multiplying monthly discharge with minimum concentration (annual mean – SD) as well as maximum concentration (annual mean + SD) of TOC and DIC of both Table 4.
