In another experiment, 96 % ethanol were heated to 70 °C (in water bath) for 2—6 minutes, otherwise "cold" (20 °C) ethanol were used. Extraction time varied from 6 to 24 hours. All samples were measured spectrophotometrically after refiltering the pigment extract through Whatman GF/C filters (25 mm) as described in Riemann & Ernst (1982). A Beckmann 26 spectrophotometer was used (1 cm cuvettes). Maximum absorbance in the red region of the spectrum was at 665 nm for chlorophyll-a in absolute methanol and 96 % ethanol. Corrections for turbidity were made by subtracting the absorbance at 750 nm which never exceeded 5 % of the 665 nm measurements. Maximum absorbance for chlorophyll-b was at 650 nm and 652 nm in ethanol and methanol, respectively. The following specific absorption coefficients were applied: chlorophyll-a in ethanol 83.4 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965), in methanol 77.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) cm (Riemann 1978), and chlorophyll-b in ethanol 45.9 l g\(^{-1}\)cm\(^{-1}\) (Winthermans & Demots 1965). Reproducibility of the chlorophyll measurements was tested using two phytoplankton cultures and one natural phytoplankton population. The coefficient of variation ranged from 1.7 % to 7.8 % (n = 10). Analysis of data were performed using Student t-test and two-factor analysis of variance (P < 0.05). Results and discussion The extraction efficiency of ethanol Two experiments were set up to compare the extraction efficiencies of ethanol and methanol. In the first experiment, four species of green algae and one natural population of phytoplankton were extracted for 6 hours in 96 % ethanol and absolute methanol. In addition, the pigments were extracted in hot and cold ethanol for various times. Except for Scenedesmus and Chlorella in stationary phases, no significant differences were found in the amount of chlorophyll-a extracted from any of the cultures, regardless solvent, heating procedure or length of extraction period (Fig. 1A—D). Furthermore, no significant differences were observed between the methanol, cold and hot ethanol extractions in the natural population of phytoplankton (Fig. 1 E). The chlorophyll-a extracted from Scenedesmus after 6 hours using hot ethanol was 54 % higher than after 6 hours methanol extraction (Fig. 1F). No significant differences were observed after 6 hours using methanol and cold ethanol, but the chlorophyll-a concentration in cold ethanol increased during the extraction period, and after 24 hours the chlorophyll concentration was 46 % higher, compared with the results obtained from methanol extraction. There were no significant differences between the extracted chlorophyll-a concentrations after 18 hours in cold and hot ethanol. Assuming that 6 hours is a sufficient extraction period using methanol (Riemann & Ernst 1982), the results obtained from Chlorella (in log phase), Selenastrum, Pediastrum and the natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø suggested a complete extraction after 6 hours in cold Fig. 1 A—F. Chlorophyll-a (mg l^{-1}) extracted from various algae cultures using absolute methanol for 6 hours or 96% cold and hot ethanol for 6, 12, 18 and 24 hours. Chlorella vulgaris was extracted during both stationary and exponential growth phase, Selenastrum capricornutum, Pediastrum duplex, and Scenedesmus quadricauda during exponential growth phase. The sample after 12 hours extraction using Pediastrum was lost. Black columns represent methanol, white columns cold ethanol, and hatched columns hot ethanol extrations (n = 3). Bars represent standard deviations. ethanol. In contrast, methanol extraction of Scenedesmus was not efficient enough to remove chlorophyll-a from the cells, since hot ethanol gave more chlorophyll-a than the cold solvents. In a similar experiment Nusch (1980) reported that methanol and ethanol were equally efficient and always more efficient than acetone. This is in contradiction to the results reported by Arvola (1981), who found that methanol was superior to ethanol. Riemann & Ernst (1982) demonstrated that methanol extracted more chlorophyll-a from Scenedesmus acutus compared with ethanol extractions. Thus, extraction efficiencies for the various solvents may be species specific. According to our results a 6 hour extraction in cold ethanol, without further treatment, is sufficient to complete the extraction in most cases. When certain green algae are dominating, longer extraction time or heating the solvents may be necessary. In a second experiment, the extraction efficiency of cold ethanol was compared with methanol extraction on natural populations of phytoplankton, to investigate the influence of phytoplankton composition on the extraction efficiency. Based on the first experiment, an 18 hour extraction time was chosen. No significant differences were found between the results obtained from ethanol or methanol extractions (Table 2), except in the samples from Ellesø and Thorsø. In Ellesø, 7% more chlorophyll was extracted with ethanol than with methanol, and in Thorsø the methanol extraction gave 3% more chlorophyll than the ethanol extraction. Table 2. To investigate the influence of temperature on the extraction efficiency, samples from 6 different lakes were heated for 2 to 6 minutes and the results were compared with results obtained from cold ethanol extraction (Table 3). The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested. Fig. 2 A—C. Chlorophyll-a (mg l\(^{-1}\)) extracted from *Chlorella vulgaris*, *Scenedesmus quadricauda* and a natural population of phytoplankton from Frederiksborg Slotssø, using varying percentages of ethanol (diluted with distilled water). Bars represent standard deviations (n = 3). When the ethanol concentration was reduced from 96% to 83.5%, 10% less chlorophyll was extracted from *Chlorella*, 14% less from the natural population of phytoplankton, and 25% less from *Scenedesmus* (Fig. 2). The relative large reduction in chlorophyll extracted from *Scenedesmus* is probably related to its morphology, which increases the possibility of water adhesion to the cells. Furthermore, the results in Fig. 2 are underestimated, since the true water content on filters containing algae, bacteria, and detritus is higher than those predicted from experiments using distilled water. Previous findings have demonstrated that the extraction efficiencies in methanol (Rie- MANN 1980) and ethanol (NUSCH 1980), were reduced when the water content was increased. Thus, the water content in ethanol extraction should be kept as low as possible. Spectrophotometric interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol Pigment extracts from natural populations of phytoplankton often contain chlorophyll-b and -c, which have absorption maxima close to that of chlorophyll-a in the red region of the spectrum. The interference from chlorophyll-b leads to an overestimation of chlorophyll-a, while the interference of chlorophyll-c in most cases may be ignored, since the absorption maximum of chlorophyll-c is 30—35 nm from the absorption peak of chlorophyll-a (MARKER et al. 1980). To investigate the interference of chlorophyll-b on the determination of chlorophyll-a in ethanol, the absorption at 665 nm was read at different mixed solutions of the two pigments (Table 4). When chlorophyll-b constituted from 5 % to 100 % of the chlorophyll-a (by weight), the absorbance at 665 nm increased from 1.5 % to 35.1 %. In similar experiments using methanol RIEMANN (1978) found an 1.4 % to 44.6 % overestimation, when chlorophyll-b constituted 5 % to 90 % of the chlorophyll-a content. This interference is higher than for ethanol, because the maximum absorbance of chlorophyll-b is closer to the peak of chlorophyll-a in methanol. LOFTUS & CARPENTER (1971) reported, that chlorophyll-b rarely constituted more than 10—20 % of the chlorophyll-a content in natural populations of phytoplankton, dominated by green algae or other algae containing chlorophyll-b. Only in one sample they found 40 % chlorophyll-b. RIEMANN & ERNST (1982) investigated six green algae and found, after optimal extraction, that chlorophyll-b constituted 13—33 % of the chlorophyll-a in methanol extracts. Table 4. Assuming that chlorophyll-b will constitute at most 30% of chlorophyll-a in natural populations of phytoplankton, the maximum interference of chlorophyll-b leads to an 9.3% overestimation of chlorophyll-a in ethanol. To correct for this interference involves either 1) a detailed spectrophotometric determination at different wavelengths (Strickland & Parsons 1972), or 2) a chromatographic separation of the chlorophylls. The first method is not recommended (Marker et al. 1980) because chlorophyll-a thereby is overestimated and a chromatographic separation is still not applicable in routine measurements. As a consequence, it is suggested that interference from chlorophyll-b in ethanol extracts may be ignored when chlorophyll-a is determined from phytoplankton. The hot ethanol extractions were generally more efficient than the cold ethanol, but no significant differences were found except from Skanderborg Lillesø, where 10—15 % more chlorophyll was obtained by heating for 2 to 6 minutes, and from Ellesø after 4 minutes. The results from the natural populations of phytoplankton support the conclusion that cold ethanol is an equally efficient extraction solvent as methanol. In the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø, which was totally dominated by *Scenedesmus*, more chlorophyll was obtained by heating the solvent. It is known from the literature that different treatments such as homogenization, ultrasonic treatments and heating (Holm-Hansen & Riemann 1978, Nusch 1980, Riemann & Ernst 1982) optimize the extraction conditions, especially when algae belonging to Chlorophyceae and Cyanophyceae dominate. However, the pigment concentration in the samples from Skanderborg Lillesø was extremely high and this may have reduced the extraction efficiency and furthermore caused an increased amount of water in the solvent, which also result in reduced extraction efficiency (see below). The effect of water content in the extraction solvent The effect of water in the ethanol was tested on *Chlorella, Scenedesmus* and on a natural population of phytoplankton. When distilled water was passed through GF/C filters during the standard procedure, the retained water was 0.139 ml (SD = 0.006; n = 3) on 25 mm GF/C filters, and 0.396 ml (SD = 0.003; n = 3) on 47 mm GF/C filters. This increased water content resulted in a 3—7 % reduction in the ethanol concentration. Based on these data, ethanol concentrations between 83.5 % and 96 % were tested.

Measuring the trophic status of ponds: Relationships between summer rate of periphytic net primary productivity and water physico-chemistry Lionel Sager* Laboratory of Ecology and Aquatic Biology (LEBA), University of Geneva, Chemin des Clochettes 18, CH-1206 Geneva, Switzerland ARTICLE INFO Article history: Received 2 July 2008 Received in revised form 22 December 2008 Accepted 23 December 2008 Published online 3 January 2009 Keywords: AFDW Alternative stable states Assessment Eutrophication Nitrogen Phosphorus Submerged macrophytes ABSTRACT The monitoring of the water quality is a major environmental concern and specific method of assessment needs to be addressed for ponds. Among threats on freshwater, eutrophication remains an important and widespread problem. To assess if the trophic state of ponds can be significantly predicted by physico-chemical surrogates, parallel measurements of water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) were performed on a set of nine lowland Swiss ponds representing the whole spectrum of trophic states. The developed methods to measure periphytic NPP on artificial substrates give similar values between the pseudo-replicates and are functional for ponds. The winter concentration of total nitrogen (TN) in the water is a significant predictor of the average summer rates of NPP while in submerged macrophyte beds total phosphorus (TP) is a better predictor. Rates of NPP measured in open water were most often higher and water transparency lower than in macrophyte beds, highlighting the positive influence of macrophytes on water quality and a possible co-occurrence in a pond of contrasting conditions when submerged species are present. This emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds to improve the water quality. 1. Introduction Monitoring and quality improvement of surface freshwater are major environmental concerns worldwide (Johnson et al., 2001). In European countries, the Water Framework Directive (WFD, Council of the European Communities, 2000) provides clear objectives to obtain at least a good qualitative and quantitative status of all waters in Europe by 2015. To attain these goals, all the aquatic compartments have to be considered and assessed with specific methods to classify them into high, good, moderate, bad and poor ecological quality. As ponds are recognized as distinct aquatic compartments from rivers and lakes (Søndergaard et al., 2005a) and react in a different manner to impacts, specific methods are required for their assessment; some are currently being developed (Menetrey et al., 2005) or are already operational (Biggs et al., 2000; Boix et al., 2005; Oertli et al., 2005), review in Indermuehle et al. (2005). Moreover, recent works have established ponds as being very significant components of the freshwater resource, in terms of their contribution to both local and regional biodiversity (Murphy, 2002; Oertli et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2003), confirming their importance to the concept of integrated catchments management. Practically, however, ponds are neglected in the implementation of the WFD as many countries have set a lower size limit of 50 ha to apply the directive on water bodies (Nicolet et al., 2007). Among the current threat on freshwater, eutrophication through diffuse pollution from agriculture (Havens et al., 2001) remain as an important, widespread and even growing problem for freshwater and coastal oceans (Carpenter et al., 1999; Bronmark and Hansson, 2002; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003; Craft et al., 2007). Accelerated rates of eutrophication linked to human activities have generated much interest during the last decades and many studies have been carried out, particularly in large lakes and rivers. Notably, an international research program of OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) associated ranges of quantifiable environmental parameters to each of 5 classes of trophic state (ultra-oligotrophic, oligotrophic, mesotrophic, eutrophic, hypertrophic) that were previously attributed with an expert system to 100 northern temperate lakes. To implement the WFD in Danish lakes, Sondergaard et al. (2005b) proposed a pre-classification of lakes based on their trophic status given by the concentration of total phosphorus (TP), in order to identify biological indicators of eutrophication. Focusing on the assessment of eutrophication, one must take into account that high nutrient concentration in small lakes or ponds do not necessarily bring a high phytoplankton biomass and a turbid water as observed in larger lakes (Sondergaard et al., 2005a), because other controlling factors are implicated including a possible scale effect (Schindler, 1998). In this way, the ranges of concentrations of nutrients in the water assigned by OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982) to each trophic class for lakes are not necessarily valid for ponds. Eutrophication is historically described as a regular increase of the phytoplankton primary productivity following larger inputs of inorganic nutrients (Naumann, 1927). This emphasis that any classification of water bodies in trophic state is an artificial reading of a continuous biological process. This continuity in eutrophication process complicates the establishment of well-defined limits between classes and furthermore the assignment of biological indicators values to a trophic state (Sondergaard et al., 2005b). As already pointed out by Rodhe (1969), the trophic state is expressed by a rate and must be determined by measuring primary production. Thus measuring rates of primary production in ponds varying in water concentration of major nutrients would permit to determine which parameters are best correlated and best predictors of the measured production and so eutrophication, even if these parameters are not the only factors determining the primary productivity as early underlined by Naumann (1932). Additionally, eutrophication is coupled at least in lakes by a shift from the dominance of benthic to pelagic production (Sand-Jensen and Borum, 1991; Vadeboncoeur et al., 2003). As the rate of primary productivity can be spatially and temporally heterogeneous for a given water body (Liboriussen and Jeppesen, 2006), a simple physico-chemical surrogate valid for ponds would be very valuable for ecological assessment. To record primary productivity in ponds varying in trophic status, the chosen method must be standardized and usable on the full range of trophic conditions. Ponds have generally a high littoral surface area relative to their pelagic volume and therefore an important potential for macrophyte and periphyton growth (Wetzel, 1990). For that reason, the benthic contribution to primary production can be more important in shallow systems like ponds than in deep lakes. Taking this benthic fraction into account is of prime importance, particularly for oligotrophic systems where it can represent the majority of the primary production (Vadeboncoeur et al., 2002). In addition, measuring periphytic productivity rather than macrophyte biomass could be more pertinent as the development of submerged vegetation is known to be discontinuous along trophic gradients (Scheffer, 1990). Moreover, Smoot et al. (1998) have shown that on artificial substrate the response of periphyton growth to nutrients is similar to the response of phytoplankton, making periphyton a valuable descriptor of phytoplankton response. This property allows the use of this indicator on the full spectrum of trophic conditions as it can grow in ponds with oligotrophic to hypertrophic conditions, where planktonic algae become the main producers and replace the benthic fraction. To focus on water quality, submerged macrophytes have the capacity to link the sediment with the overlying water and so to mobilize nutrients from the sediments (Graneli and Solander, 1988), in contrast to periphyton that cannot directly uptake nutrients stocked in the sediment (except for the epipelon (Hansson, 1992)). To standardize the measure of periphytic productivity, independent of the grazing pressure by zooplankton and macroinvertebrates, it has to be performed in controlled conditions with no access to grazers. Furthermore, the measurement must take into account the presence of macrophyte beds. Actually these can influence the abundance of periphyton by several mechanisms, notably competition for nutrient resources, release of allelopathic substances (Wium-Andersen, 1987; Ervin and Wetzel, 2003; Gross et al., 2003) or sheltering of the zooplanktonic and macroinvertebrate communities from predation (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997). Moreover, parallel measurements of periphytic productivity performed outside and inside beds of submerged plants permit to calculate a mean value of productivity between results obtained in open water and in macrophyte beds and also to detect potential co-occurrence within a pond of contrasting conditions linked by a continuous gradient between clear water zone colonized by submerged macrophytes and turbid zone without submerged vegetation. Co-occurring contrasting conditions have already been described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes of greater surfaces than the ponds considered here. Since there is an important nutrient recycling and rapid turnover in ponds and other shallow systems, water concentrations of nutrients show considerable fluctuation during the growing season, and a large part are mobilized in the biota and are not measurable in the water. During winter however, for ponds located at medium and high latitude, biological activity and primary productivity are very low and nutrients are in the water column for the most part, in dissolved or particle forms (Linton and Goulder, 2000). Hansson (1992) notably observed the peak of total phosphorus (TP) in open water occurring during winter for high latitudes lakes. Thus, winter values are expected to give a better picture of the potential of primary productivity by quantifying the amounts available in spring for the growth of producers. Furthermore, winter values avoid the confounding effects of uptake of phosphorus and denitrification that occur with summer readings (James et al., 2005). By performing parallel measurements of winter water physico-chemistry and of summer rates of periphytic productivity on a small dataset of ponds, this study aims to: 1) identify correlations between periphytic productivity and physico-chemical indicators of the trophic state, 2) detect a possible co-occurrence of contrasting conditions of turbidity and periphytic productivity in a given pond, 3) assess if a single chemical surrogate of primary productivity can potentially be used to classify ponds in the same biogeographic area according to their trophic state. Such a surrogate could serve as a basis to calibrate ecological value by species and select biological metrics of eutrophication. Additionally, this study will provide an opportunity to test the reliability of the method adapted for measuring the periphytic net primary productivity in ponds. 2. Material and methods 2.1. Study sites This study took place in the western part of the Swiss Plateau, a distinct biogeographic area (sensus Gonseth et al., 2001). The landscape of this area, where human population and agriculture are concentrated, has been intensely modified during the 20th century by increase in urbanisation and the intensification of agricultural practices (Lundstrom-Gillieron and Schlaepfer, 2003), resulting in the fragmentation of natural areas. The nine permanent ponds surveyed for this analysis represent a gradient of primary productivity from oligomesotrophic to hypertrophic. These ponds, located between 420 and 773 m a.s.l, are small and shallow, ranging from 327 to 10,616 m^2 in surface area, (mean: 3087 m^2, median: 2733 m^2) and from 0.38 to 1.03 m in mean depths (mean and median: 0.7 m). All these sites are colonized by fish. Four of the nine water bodies are colonized by submerged species of macrophytes (S), three by floating-leaves species (F) but without submerged hydrophytes and two supports only emerged vegetation (E). The location and the main morphometric characteristics of the ponds are given in Fig. 1 and Table 1. The sampling of the vegetation was made with the standardized method of Oertli et al. (2005) and consists of prospection by square quadrats (0.25 m^2) disposed equidistantly along transects perpendicular to the longest axis of the pond and located at regular intervals according to the pond size. The minimum number of quadrat prospected per pond (n) is related to the water surface area (m^2) by the equation \( n = 1.96 - 2.8 \times \log_{10}(\text{area}) + 2.6 \times (\log_{10}(\text{area}))^2 \). Such a strategy was shown to sample at least 70% of the real richness. A specie list was noted for each quadrat along with abundance in semi-quantitative classes. The number of quadrats prospected and the main species of macrophytes by site are given in Table 2 along with an estimation of their abundance at the pond scale. ![Map showing the study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds.](page_1092_186_1017_670.png) Fig. 1 – Study area in the western part of Switzerland and location of the ponds. 2.2. Periphytic primary productivity Rates of periphytic net primary productivity (NPP) on artificial substrates and in absence of herbivores (method adapted from Clesceri et al., 1998; Chase, 2003) were directly recorded in situ in each pond as a measure of periphytic primary productivity at two points chosen with criterion detailed thereafter. All measures were performed at location with similar water depths (0.8 m) and in areas with minimal shading from terrestrial vegetation or from surrounding plants for measures in macrophyte beds. In all cases the shading at the location of the measurement point never attain five percent of the surface. Measurements were performed continuously from June 6, 2005 to August 2, 2005, across the period of longest daytime in northern hemisphere and until the aquatic vegetation biomass summer peak (Jackson et al., 1994). This period correspond to the time of optimal growth conditions for periphyton on artificial substrate as identified by Jobgen et al. (2004). Submerged macrophyte presence in four ponds and floating-leaves species presence in three ponds were taken into account by measuring productivity inside vegetation stands and in open water. Growth rates were determined by measuring the accumulation of periphyton on the inner side of transparent plastic boxes (polystyrene PS) offering each a colonisable surface of 0.023 m^2 (Fig. 2). Boxes were covered by a net on their open face (mesh size 0.25 mm) to prevent, or at least limit the income of grazers, and were positioned two to three centimeters below the water surface in groups of three pseudo-replicates fixed around a pole planted in the pond base. According to Chase and Ryberg (2004), such a mesh retains about 10% of the available light “but did not significantly reduce algal growth in a controlled experiment performed in the absence of grazers”. Preventing the access of grazers is of prime importance for this study and as Jones et al. (2002) pointed out, the grazing pressure is a stronger limiting factor of the net production of periphyton than the water nutrient concentration. To reduce to the minimum meteorologically related variation among ponds, sampling and replacement of the boxes of all nine ponds were carried out over the shortest possible time period (two days). 2.3. Physico-chemistry Water physico-chemistry was measured once in winter and physical parameters were measured five times in summer (at each box replacement). The winter fieldwork was undertaken during three consecutive days (from 9 to 11 February, 2005) after a long frost period. Water sampling and field measurements were made at the deeper central point of each pond by drilling a hole in the ice cover. Water samples were taken at 20 cm below the icy surface with a sampling bottle, and then stocked in acid pre-rinse PE plastic bottles immediately before being stored in the dark in a refrigerated box. Water samples for the analysis of dissolved components (PO₄-P (soluble reactive phosphorus = SRP), NO₃-N, NH₃-N) were filtered in situ trough 0.45 μm filters (Schleicher & Schuell ME 25). Unfiltered samples were kept for total phosphorus (TP) and total nitrogen (TN) analyses. All samples were stored in the dark at 4 °C and analysed within 48 h after field collection. The SESA water quality laboratory (VD) analyzed all the water samples with standard methods. TP was determined after potassium persulphate digestion at 121 °C and under pressure for half an hour; SRP was further measured by the ascorbate acid/molybdenum blue method (Clesceri et al., 1998). TN was determined by chemiluminescence after oxidization in NO at high temperature and reaction with ozone. NH₃-N was determined by colorimetry with the salicylate method. NO₃-N was determined by ion chromatography. A deep profile was made in the field for physical parameters (temperature, pH, conductivity) using a multi-parameters probe (YSI 556®, YSI Incorporated, Yellowspring, USA). Water turbidity (NTU) and transparency (cm) were also measured in the field with a turbidity meter (WTW Turb 355 IR®, WTW GmbH, Weilheim, D) and a Snellen tube of 60 cm length. 2.4. Data analyses To assess the reliability of the primary productivity measurement method, mean rate of productivity and variance were calculated for each measurement point and sampling occasion. In parallel, productivity rates by pseudo-replicates were box-plotted by point and sampling occasion to visually detect eventual outliers. To test if any measured physical and chemical variables could explain the differences of periphytic productivity among ponds, multiple stepwise linear regressions were performed (threshold of entry \( p \leq 0.05 \), removal \( \geq 0.1 \)). As we wanted to explore the relationships between summer periphytic growth rate and winter concentrations of TP or TN, linear stepwise regressions were performed with these two parameters in a first set of predictors and physical parameters in a second set to see if their inclusion could improve the \( R^2 \) and significance of the models. Regressions were performed between seasonal productivity rates of each pond and the corresponding mean of physical parameters of the water as well as winter concentrations of nutrients. Mean productivity rate by pond is the sum of the means of the two sampling points of each sampling occasion. To refine the regressions according to the sampling points, the same above procedure was applied separately for three subsets of the data (open water (O), submerged species (S) and floating-leaves species (F)). As one of the ponds shows very high rates of productivity, we reapplied the whole procedure after removing this extreme value from the dataset to verify if the identified regressions remained significant. The critical \( \alpha \) values were corrected by applying the Bonferroni corrections for non-independent comparisons (Maxwell and Delaney, 1990). As a second objective we wanted to compare the rates of periphytic productivity between sampling points located in the same pond, respectively inside versus outside macrophyte stands. With all sampling occasions, there were enough data to test the significance of the differences among locations with an unparametric test (Mann–Whitney) between productivity by boxes at the sampling points. As there were not enough pseudo-replicates to validate the statistical test by sampling occasion, simple box plot by sampling points and by sampling occasion were plotted for each pond. This revealed if differences were detectable, and helped rank productivity rates at each vegetated sampling point in space and time as lower, equal or higher to unvegetated points. 3. Results The set of ponds display a wide range of periphytic growth rate, nutrient concentrations and water physical parameters. Measures of periphytic growth rate by single point and sampling occasion ranged from 0.022 to 48.406 gC/m²/14 days (0.0016–3.458 gC/m²/day) and the mean seasonal value for ponds ranged from 1.284 to 52.950 gC/m²/56 days (0.023– 0.946 gC/m²/day). The daily mean seasonal value by point and by pond and the mean value by point and by sampling occasions are given in Table 3 along with variance between pseudo-replicates, except for the first sampling occasions where the three boxes by point were weighted together. Rates for the last sampling occasion in open water of pond P3 could not be retained for the analyses because the boxes emerged during sampling. Six exposed boxes were also damaged and the measurements were removed from the dataset. Winter nutrient concentrations of TP ranged from 0.002 to 0.346 mg L⁻¹ and TN varied from 0.7 to 5.83 mg L⁻¹. Ranges and mean values for summer and winter measurements of physico-chemical parameters are given in Table 4 3.1. Regressions of productivity rates with physico-chemical parameters The mean seasonal rates of periphytic primary productivity by pond defined as the sum of the mean value by pond for each sampling occasion are positively correlated to the water concentration of total nitrogen (TN) measured during the previous winter (linear regression for the whole season, Table 5, model 1, \( r^2 = 0.974, p = 8.55e-07 \)). With the stepwise procedure, the regression remained the same with winter TN as unique predictor. Without the extreme value of the hypertrophic site (P6), the regression between the seasonal productivity by pond and the winter concentration of TN remained valid, even if less significant and less strong (model 2, Table 5, \( r^2 = 0.754, p = 5.16e-03 \)). In that case, the stepwise regression retained the mean water transparency as second predictor negatively correlated with productivity, improving the performance of the model (model 3, Table 5). The scatter plot of the seasonal values of productivity versus TN or TP presented in Fig. 3 shows additionally the OECD (Vollenweider and Kerekes, 1982; Wetzel, 1983; Forsberg and Ryding, 1980) limits of nutrient concentration between trophic classes as well as the limits between the classes of ecological quality included for shallow lakes by Sondergaard et al. (2005b). For the measures located in open water, regressions with TN were also significant for seasonal productivity (model 1, Table 6, \( r^2 = 0.937, p = 1.68e-05 \)). The stepwise procedure even improves the model by including the mean turbidity as second predictor (model 2 Table 6). Without the upper value of productivity (pond P6), the regressions are less strong but the predictors remain the same.

Discussion 4.1. Reliability and limitations of the method for ponds The rates of productivity measured for each pseudo-replicate for a given point and sampling occasion were similar even if the variance between the boxes increased for high means (see Table 3 and Fig. 4). Despite this uncontrolled effect, the method is sensitive and allows classifying ponds of this dataset by trophic states characterized by TN as a higher variance between pseudo-replicates occurs in systems already hypertrophic. However as the data material is small and restricted to a limited geographic area, these results need to be confirmed on a broader scale to generalize this outcome for ponds in the area. Observed rates (Table 3) were low compared with other studies (for instance see Chase (2003) with measured productivity ranging between 6.12 and 56.2 g/m²/day). This could be due to the smaller net mesh size used to cover the open face of boxes, which could have limited the colonization by algae. On the other hand this net allowed inter-sites comparisons by strongly reducing and homogenising the residual grazing factor. The nature of the artificial substrate can also be involved. Actually, the review of Cattaneo and Amireault (1992) suggested that the type of artificial substrate is not crucial but Danilov and Ekelund (2001) observed no growth of periphyton on PVC substrate and the formation of a slim layer of bacteria covering the artificial substrate. No such layer was observed in the current study and the poly-styrene plastic often employed in biology, notably for the Petri dishes, is more likely to have played an inhibitory effect as it seems to be the case with PVC. 4.2. Periphytic productivity and nutrients The significant positive regression observed between TN and mean periphytic growth rate is consistent with other studies, for instance Luttenton and Lowe (2006) found significant correlation between nitrogen concentration on nutrient-diffusive substrata (NDS) and total biovolume of periphyton growing on this substrate. Similarly Chase and Ryberg (2004) found positive correlations between primary productivity measured with a method similar to this study and TP and TN in order of importance. Kahlert and Pettersson (2002) also measured an increase in the biomass of benthic algae with trophic levels even if it was not correlated with the nutrient status of the algae itself. Moreover, rooted plants can obtain phosphorus from the sediment and in this way act as a source for the water column (Carignan and Kalff, 1982) while nitrogen on the other hand tends to be lost through denitrification within plant stands (Weisner et al., 1994). Peretyatko et al. (2007) observed notably that dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) tends to decrease in pond water during the warmer month, especially in sites without submerged species and abundant phytoplankton. Therefore, in shallow lakes with macrophyte stands, algal populations can be nitrogen limited during summer (Moss et al., 2005) even if, as in this study, the winter TN/TP ratio does not indicate a nitrogen limitation in most of the ponds. Additionally, on NDS spanning a large range of molar N/P ratios and nutrient concentrations, Luttenton and Lowe (2006) showed that nitrogen concentration is a significant predictor of the algal biovolume growing on the substrate and that neither the N/P ratio nor the phosphorus concentration of the NDS were significantly correlated with this biovolume. These results suggest that the TP concentration measured in winter is an underestimation of the available phosphorus during the growing season. As all the ponds were icy at the time of the winter sampling, the absence of turbulence under the ice cover should have limited the suspension of fine particles in the water column. During warm months with a high water temperature and a low concentration of dissolved oxygen, ponds with organic P-saturated sediment can be net source of P by release of the iron-bound P (Søndergaard et al., 1999; Fairchild and Velinsky, 2006). Conversely the winter concentrations of TN could be an over estimation of the available nutrient in summer as a significant part can be lost through denitrification. This could explain the relatively high concentrations of TN and the corresponding trophic levels attributed to the ponds when compared to the TP concentrations and corresponding trophic classes (Fig. 3). It is therefore likely that the trophic status of the ponds is overestimated when the limits of Wetzel (1983) or Forsberg and Ryding (1980) set for large lakes are directly applied to the winter concentration of TN as in Fig. 3. On the other hand the limits of nutrient concentration proposed by Søndergaard et al. (2005b) to set ecological quality classes for shallow lakes (Fig. 3, dashed lines) seems to be more appropriate for ponds. In particular, it reassigned the sites classified as eutrophic following the TP or TN scales of Vollenweider and Kerekes (1982), Forsberg and Ryding (1980) and Wetzel (1983) into moderate to good quality, and the mesotrophic sites into high quality while keeping the hypertrophic ponds in poor to bad quality classes. These scales, even if not giving a trophic status, rely directly on water quality and distribute the gradient of nutrient concentrations observed in ponds in all the quality classes based either on TP or TN. 4.3. Roles and effects of submerged macrophytes The observed lower rates of periphytic productivity within boxes placed in the submerged macrophyte stands of two truly stagnant sites harboring continuously submerged species show the influences of submerged plants on nutrient cycling. Notably, macrophytes and their associated epiphytes mobilize and store nutrients prior to releasing it during their senescence. This competitive storage involves a reduced nutrient availability for phytoplankton (Kufel and Ozimek, 1994) and for the periphyton colonizing the artificial substrate. These results are concordant with the observation of Takamura et al. (2003) who found at a similar nutrient level a significantly lower concentration of planktonic chlorophyll within submerged macrophytes than in lakes without submerged species. Similarly, Liboriussen and Jeppesen (2003) and Vadeboncoeur et al. (2001) observed lower gross primary productivity in clear water compared to turbid one. When measuring biomass of phytoplankton, Peretyatko et al. (2007) reported lower amount in ponds supporting submerged plants when compared to unvegetated ponds or those with floating-leaved species only. With a measure of the total lake net primary production, Blindow et al. (2006) observed higher level in a clear lake compared to a turbid one but the two lakes considered in that study were deeper than the ponds considered here, and their water column, if turbid, experienced more self-shading and higher rates of community respiration than shallower sites. In fact, Blindow et al. (2006) pointed out that this difference of total net primary productivity between clear and turbid water tends to decrease with the mean depth by reducing the water volume below the compensation depth. As the artificial substrates used in our study were set 2–3 cm below the water surface, the measured growths of periphyton are less influenced by phytoplankton shading. The contrasting conditions of turbidity and transparency observed between macrophyte stands and open water were previously described by Scheffer et al. (1994) in shallow lakes. Other factors could also explain the lower periphytic productivity rates often measured within plant stands, for example shading by the macrophytes canopy (Ozimek et al., 1990), strong evidence of release of allelopathic substances by macrophytes (Gross et al., 2007) or increased rates of sedimentation (Carpenter, 1981; Petticrew et al., 1991) accompanied by a reduced resuspension within macrophyte stands (Scheffer et al., 1993). A lower or a negative net production of the epiphyte communities colonizing the artificial substrate placed within submerged species, as seasonally observed on natural substrate by Vis et al. (2006), can also explain the difference between open water and macrophyte stands. If the respiration process is more important than in open water, the amount of carbon measured after two weeks underestimates primary production. Conversely, the refuge effect of submerged macrophyte for grazers (Timms and Brian, 1984; Jeppesen et al., 1997) must be here less important as the experimental design that we used strongly limit the influence of large macroinvertebrates grazers. On one of the four sites harboring submerged species (P5), the early senescence of Myriophyllum spicatum (represented by the upward arrow in Fig. 4) during the second part of June was accompanied by a strong increase in the rate of productivity at the corresponding location that even surpasses the rate measured in open water. This is probably due to the direct recycling of nutrients released by macrophytes as periphyton can directly exploit this resource (Cattaneo and Kalff, 1979; Carignan and Kalff, 1982; Rooney and Kalff, 2003). Moreover, Carpenter (1980) but also Smith and Adams (1986) showed that the importance of macrophyte-derived nutrients for epiphyton increases with the degree of senescence of the plant. Additionally, Carignan and Kalff (1982) have specifically measured that M. spicatum is a significant source of highly available P for the surrounding epiphyton and phytoplankton. Interestingly, the water transparency remains inversely correlated to the rate of primary productivity and became simultaneously lower within macrophytes than in open water (data not shown). This peak of productivity was follow by a rapid growth of dense beds of Ceratophyllum demersum in early July along with a reduction of the rate measured in the box even if transparency remained low (downward arrow in Fig. 4). During this period, the rate of productivity continued to increase in open water to reach the seasonal peak during the first fortnight of July (Fig. 4). This delayed growth in open water compared to the growth measured in senescing beds during the previous two weeks can be linked to the horizontal diffusion from beds to open water of the available nutrients, similarly to what was observed by Rooney and Kalff (2003) studying active cycling from the sediment mediated by macrophytes. During the last fortnight of July, open water was progressively colonized by stands of C. demersum generating a net reduction in the productivity rate and resulting in similar values between the two sampling points becoming gradually both vegetated. The site P9 is a bit different as it has a flow-through regime, which is not the case in the other sites. In this case the mean rates of productivity were higher in macrophyte stands than in open water (118.7%–226.5% of the rates measured in open water). As already mentioned, measured rates as well as absolute differences were very low and the values were even overlapping between pseudo-replicates of the two sampling points (Fig. 4). Nevertheless, this trend differs notably from the other sites characterized by well-marked differences in periphytic productivity measured in the boxes between plant stands and open water. This difference can be due to different factors, notably a lower current speed through the dense macrophyte stands (Gessner, 1950; Stephan and Gutknecht, 2002) increasing the water retention time and potentially enhancing both sedimentation and the use of dissolved nutrients. Other factors could be involved, notably a release of nutrients by macrophytes, as mentioned earlier. Actually, this pond exhibits low concentration of dissolved nutrients (Table 4) and the nutritive contribution of healthy plants to periphyton, even if little, is known to be more important in oligotrophic water (Eminson and Moss, 1980; Burkholder and Wetzel, 1990). Additionally, nutrient diffusion may be facilitated and mixing of the water mediated by the current tends to also homogenize the conditions across the site. In this pond, transparency was always at the maximum value at the two sampling points and the turbidity remained low in value and range (inferior to four NTU among all measurements). 5. Conclusions and perspectives Firstly, the method of periphytic productivity measurement adapted in this study operates well with this dataset of ponds and gives repeatable measures except for the hypertrophic sites that showed an increase of the variance between pseudo-replicates. Secondly the results indicated that for the study area considered, the winter concentration of total nitrogen was a significant predictor of the summer rates of periphytic productivity measured in open water or averaged by ponds. When beds of submerged macrophytes were present, the periphytic productivity within the plant stands was generally lower and the transparency higher. In that case, the winter concentration of TP was a stronger and better predictor of the productivity. This limited growth of periphyton within the boxes placed in submerged macrophyte beds puts in evidence for the positive effects of submerged plants on water quality and emphasizes the importance of maintaining or restoring submerged macrophyte stands in ponds. Extending these results for assessing pond water quality in other region of Switzerland would require a similar study on a broader scale notably with sites located at higher altitudes, as the range of environmental parameters of particular concern for primary productivity differs broadly between Alps and lowlands (Hinden et al., 2005). monitoring_status.full_text:
Monitoring status, habitat features and amphibian species richness of Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds at the edge of the species range (Salzburg, Austria) A. Maletzky1*, M. Kyek2, A. Goldschmid1 1 University of Salzburg, Department of Organismic Biology, Hellbrunnerstrasse 34, A-5020 Salzburg. 2 Institute of Ecology, Johann Herbst Strasse 23, A-5061 Elsbethen. We studied the status of Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds in the province of Salzburg during the years 2004 and 2005. Historical and current distribution data were collected and compared. In the end of 2004, 51 ponds with Crested newt records of which 39 still existed were known in Salzburg. In 2005 we carried out a monitoring of these ponds using a combination of three survey methods. Presence or absence of adult and larval Crested newts and the number of syntopic amphibian species were recorded. Detection probabilities and the effects of seven characteristic pond features on pond occupancy were calculated for adult and larval newts separately. We observed a strong decline of ponds occupied by Crested newts with presence of adults in 22 and presence of larvae in 16 surveyed ponds, respectively. Detection probabilities imply that we detected all ponds occupied by adults and larvae. Key habitat features for Crested newt presence are low degree of shading for adults and larvae as well as a high density of submerged vegetation for larvae. Pond size and depth are not significant. Furthermore we recorded a significantly higher number of amphibian species in ponds occupied by Crested newts. Our results might aid in the implementation of sustainable measures for a conservation of these critically endangered species in the province of Salzburg. Keywords: Habitat features, monitoring, pond occupancy, Salzburg, Triturus cristatus superspecies. Introduction During the past decades a decline of amphibian populations in many parts of the world has been observed (e.g. Wake 1991, Houlahan et al. 2000). There are several hypotheses to account for this decline on the global scale. Most probably a combination of many factors is responsible (Collins & Storfer 2003). In the case of the highly urbanised and developed countries of Central and Western Europe, the major factor is without doubt the loss of natural and functioning pond networks (Oertli et al. 2005), due to destruction and manipulation of wetlands and ponds (e.g. Corbett 1989, Beebee 1997, Wood et al. 2003). The province of Salzburg (Austria) consists of a variety of habitats within a vertical range of 380 to 3600 m above sea level. Hence there exists a great variety of pond types facing many different threats. Especially in the lowland areas of the North and the inner alpine river valleys, the number of ponds in natural conditions has decreased throughout the past decades due to intensive anthropogenic pressure and land use. Most of the remaining ponds are artificial and often densely stocked with fish and waterfowl (Kyek & Maletzky 2006). At present the occurrence of 15 amphibian species is documented, of which 13 are reproducing in standing water bodies. Four species have been classified as critically endangered in the current regional Red List of amphibians and reptiles, including the two occurring Crested newt species (Triturus cristatus, Laurenti 1768 and Triturus carnifex, Laurenti 1768) (Kyek & Maletzky 2006). Crested newts (Triturus cristatus superspecies) are distributed over great parts of Europe with populations showing significant declines in large parts of this area (Gasc et al. 1997). As these species are listed in Annex II and IV of the EU-habitats directive 92/43/EEC as well as Annex II of the Bern Convention, their conservation status is of European importance. The populations in the province of Salzburg are of special interest, being located in a part of their distribution areas, where the two species can be found narrowly sympatric and hybrid populations exist (e.g. Freytag, 1978, Thiesmeier & Kupfer 2000, Arntzen 2003). For this study we therefore stick to the taxon Triturus cristatus superspecies. The results of a survey on the identification of the species using molecular methods are in preparation (Maletzky unpublished data). Due to their wide distribution area Crested newts inhabit a variety of pond types. Generally these water bodies can be described as large and deep with submerged vegetation and absence of fish (Arntzen 2003). The characteristics of suitable ponds depend more on the particular landscape features than on the particular species (e.g. Cabela & Grillitsch 2001, Arntzen 2003). The quality and quantity of these characteristics in part determines the presence and size of the populations (Oldham et al. 2000). Monitoring the distribution and the key habitat features is among the most important requirements for the effective conservation management of threatened species at regional level. A major problem with most monitoring programs is that species are detected imperfectly, which might lead to biased estimates of population trends (MacKenzie et al. 2002, Schmidt 2005). A determination of key habitat features can serve as a basis for detecting the likelihood of occurrence and a guideline for habitat enhancement and creation. Already several studies dealt with the selection and suitability of amphibian breeding habitats using multivariate analysis (Pavignano et al. 1990), discriminant analysis (Swan & Oldham 1994) or logistic regression (Laurila 1998). Key habitat criteria for Crested newt species have been evaluated mainly in core distribution areas of T. carnifex (Pavignano et al. 1990) and of T. cristatus (Oldham et al. 2000). The aims of this study are (1) to evaluate the status of Crested newts in the province of Salzburg, (2) to identify key habitat features for their occurrence in ponds, and (3) to develop standards for the creation or enhancement of ponds supporting these critically endangered species at the edge of their distribution range. Materials and methods Study area The study area covers the three northern districts of the province of Salzburg ("Salzburg Stadt", "Salzburg Land", "Hallein"), with a total area of 1777 km². The main landscape features are the valley of the lower Salzach River, parts of the northern Limestone Alps, Flysch zone and the foothills of the Alps with the lake district (Fig. 1). Historical data Although there are some historical records on the occurrence of Crested newts in Salzburg (e.g. Woltersstorff 1925, Schüller 1963, Freytag 1978), data on precise localities and structure of ponds are scarce. Some information could be drawn from unpublished mapping projects (Kyek unpublished data) and the collection of L. Schüller located in the Natural History Museum "Haus der Natur", Salzburg. Geographical coordinates (± 100-500 m) and habitat descriptions of the origin of preserved specimens were attributed to each record as precise as possible. Together with more recent records collected by the authors, Crested newts were known from 44 ponds between the years 1949 and 2003. Monitoring We examined the status of the 44 ponds with previous records of Crested newts in 2004 and carried out a monitoring of the ponds that were still existing as well as new found localities in 2005. Presence or absence of Crested newt adults and larvae as well as syntopic amphibian species was recorded during three visits per pond between April and July. We used a combination of detection methods with bottle traps, night ![Geographical distribution of monitored Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds in 2005. Solid triangle = unconfirmed localities (n = 16); Encircled solid triangles = confirmed localities (n = 22).](page_1092_320_1012_1012.png) Fig. 1 Geographical distribution of monitored Crested newt (Triturus cristatus superspecies) ponds in 2005. Solid triangle = unconfirmed localities (n = 16); Encircled solid triangles = confirmed localities (n = 22). counting and dip-netting. Bottle traps were the main tool for detection and used in each of the three surveys. Such traps are especially useful for presence-absence surveys in ponds that are big or otherwise difficult to examine (Griffiths 1985). We used a minimum number of 10 traps per pond and placed one trap at least every 5 meters. Traps were positioned mainly in shallow water areas with an angle of about 45°. A small perforated part remaining above the water surface allowed the captured individuals to breathe (H. Schedl, pers. comm.). The traps were active overnight from late afternoon to the following morning. The second visit was accompanied by additional night counting, while the third visit was especially focussed on the detection of larvae by means of dip-netting. Habitat features We recorded the particular pond type using the standardized mapping form for monitoring the Austrian herpetofauna (Kyek 1996). Furthermore we recorded 7 habitat features for Crested newt ponds including pond area (m²), maximum depth in three classes (<30 cm, 30-100 cm, >100 cm), fish presence or absence, origin (natural or artificial), and presence or absence of human use. We also estimated density of submerged vegetation (in 25 %-classes) and proportion of shade (in 25 %-classes). Data analysis All mapping and monitoring data were processed with BioOffice-databanking (©Biogis) and ArcView 9.1 for GIS (© Esri). For the monitoring data of the year 2005 we estimated detection probabilities and the proportion of sites occupied by adults and larvae separately, using the mark recapture like approach of MacKenzie et al. (2002, 2005). The analysis was done with the software Presence 2.0. The effects of habitat variables on the presence of Crested newts, adults and larvae, were analysed by means of logistic regression, which was performed with R freeware (R Development Core Team 2005). We used the Firth's bias reduced logistic regression implemented in the LOGISTF-package (Ploner et al. 2006). Results Status and monitoring of Crested newt ponds While 32 (72.7 %) ponds with old records still exist, all ponds with records before 1977 have been destroyed. In contrast, we recorded Crested newt presence in 7 ponds which were evaluated for the first time in the two study years. Therefore to date, 39 (out of a total of 51 records) Crested newt ponds are known in the province of Salzburg. One private garden pond could not be surveyed in the course of this study. During the monitoring of 38 ponds in 2005 the presence of adult Crested newts was recorded for 22 ponds (57.9 %), larvae were detected in 16 ponds (42.1 %) (Fig. 1, Tab. 1), while 16 ponds were classified as unoccupied Crested newt ponds (Tab. 2). We analysed detection probabilities for adults and larvae separately. Therefore we first tested two pre-defined models that used constant and survey-specific detection probabilities. For both adults and larvae the lower AIC value indicated that the survey-specific P model was better supported by the data and detection probabilities were time specific. The predicted site occupancy using this model was 0.588 (SE = 0.082) for adults and 0.431 (SE = 0.081) for larvae, respectively (Tab. 3). While detection probabilities (P) for adults were high in all three surveys ranging from 0.640 to 0.951, detection probabilities for larvae were very low in the first two surveys but high (i.e. P = 1.000) in the third one (Tab. 4). These results imply that we detected all the ponds where adult and larval Crested newts were present. Habitat features of studied ponds The mean water surface area of studied ponds (n = 38) was 342.2 m² (± 425.2 m² std. dev.) with a range of 20-2000 m². The majority of ponds showed maximum depths of 30-100 cm (56.4 %), while a maximum depth of more than 1 meter was recorded for 16 ponds (41.0 %). Only one pond had a maximum depth of less than 30 cm. Fish presence was recorded for 8 (21.1 %) ponds, three of them being densely stocked. Artificial ponds (71.1 %) were built for purposes like fish breeding, ice stock sliding in winter and fire protection. One brewery ice pond that was created to have a cheap possibility of cooling is now used extensively for fish breeding. Private garden ponds are used for swimming or ornamental reasons. Eight ponds (20.5 %) were created in the course of nature conservation projects since 1991. The habitat feature human use contains 25 (65.8 %) of these ponds that are periodically managed and succession is interrupted, which is beneficial for amphibian populations. Thirteen ponds (34.2 %) are not used currently and thus subject to strong succession. The proportion of average area covered by submerged vegetation was 0-25 % in 17 ponds, 26-50 % in 11 and 51-75 % in 9 ponds respectively. Only one pond had 75-100 % submerged vegetation cover. We found that a low degree of shade is the most important habitat variable with significant results in both adult (P > 0.001) and larval (P > 0.05) presence. The latter was also significantly correlated to a high density of submerged vegetation (P > 0.001), which showed a comparably high but not significant probability in adults. Altogether 8 further amphibian taxa could be detected in the surveyed ponds. Of these, Alpine newt (Mesotriton alpestris Laurenti, 1768) and Smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris L., 1758) were most frequently found in occupied Crested newt ponds (90.9 % each), while they were present in 50 % and 37.5 % of the unoccupied ponds, respectively. The Tree frog (Hyla arborea L., 1758) was detected in 59.1 % of occupied ponds, while there are no records for unoccupied ones. Likewise the Yellow bellied toad (Bombina variegata L., 1758) was only found in occupied ponds with a frequency of 31.8 %. Discussion Status and monitoring of Crested newt ponds The occurrence and frequency of Crested newts (Triturus cristatus superspecies) has declined seriously during the last century. One of the main factors for this pattern is the loss or manipulation of suitable breeding habitats (Arntzen 2003). Our study represents the first approach of a species specific monitoring of amphibian breeding ponds in the province of Salzburg. It shows that about 25 % of all recorded ponds with crested newt presence have disappeared and reproduction was observed in less than 50 % of the existing ponds. Europe have been published throughout the previous decades. In the German federal state of Rhineland-Palatinate the loss of habitats was regarded as 20 % (Bitz & Simon 1996). In Great Britain regional estimates vary widely from 90 % for parts of London to 6 % for urban ponds in Edinburgh (Wood et al. 2003). Monitoring projects of Crested newt populations in neighbouring regions showed comparably low occupation levels. In South-Eastern Bavaria 9 out of 20 surveyed ponds were found unoccupied (Gruber, H.-J. unpublished data). In the province of Lower Austria, Klepsch (1994) found Crested newt presence in only 5 out of 14 sites that were occupied ten years before. These data are similar to the decrease of 1.4 – 2.0 % in population numbers per annum which was estimated for Great Britain (Clemons 1997). The reasons for the declining number of Crested newt populations and habitats in our area are generally related to the fact that these species are restricted to the lowlands and hills in the northern districts. Their distribution area is nearly identical with the main human settlement area, which is underlying increasing pressure from infrastructure and land use. Data on current and historical vertical distribution show that most populations have been lost in the lowlands (Maletzky unpublished data). Species detection in monitoring studies tends to be imperfect especially for rare species and small populations. If populations are unequally detectable across groups to be compared, results are biased and do not reflect reality (Kery 2004). Such unequal detectability despite the use of standardised methods can for instance be caused by environmental or climatic variables. Statistical methods for estimating site occupancy are useful tools for analysing the significance of monitoring data (MacKenzie et al. 2002) and have been successfully applied for monitoring amphibian distribution in terrestrial (Bailey et al. 2004) and aquatic (Schmidt 2005) habitats. Crested newts might be missed during surveys especially when submerged vegetation is dense and deep water zones are extended (e.g. Beebee 1990). However, Cooke (1995) showed that survey results at a secure site using night counting procedures were positively related to numbers gained by bottle traps. In our study the detection probabilities for both adults and larvae were high compared to a related study dealing with three anuran species (Schmidt 2005). We did not test climatic effects on our detection histories but personal experience shows that especially bottle traps are effective independent of weather conditions. We achieved the highest detection probability for adult newts in the second survey, probably caused by the combination of night counting and bottle traps. The increasing probability in detection of larvae is most probably explained by the survey dates. Altogether the use of combined methods can in our case be regarded as adequate and successful. Habitat features of studied ponds Many studies in core distribution areas have dealt with the question what might make a good Crested newt pond (e.g. Swan & Oldham 1994, Oldham et al. 2000). According to Blab & Blab (1981) shading, pond area and density of submerged vegetation are the three relevant pond characteristics for the abundance of Crested newts. In a study from Western France shading represented a key feature for the abundance of larval Triturus newts, suggesting that the successional stage of the pond is important (Sztatecsny et al. 2004). Our results reflect these findings to a certain degree. Shading and density of submerged vegetation had significant effects on pond occupancy in our study, while pond area was of no importance for Crested newt presence. Cooke et al. (1994) regarded ponds with less than 10 % shade as ideal for populations in Great Britain. In a study from the German province of Lower Saxony Crested newts are missing from ponds with a degree of shading higher than 40 % (Filoda 1981). Although in the province of Salzburg the number of ponds located in open areas is low due to intensive land use, and most of the surveyed ponds are to some extent associated with forests or shrubberies, the majority of occupied ponds showed a degree of shading below 50 %. Positive effects of submerged vegetation density were reported by Oldham (1994) who suggested a total macrophyte cover of 70-80 % as ideal for Crested newt ponds. While in our study this effect was high but not significant for adults, we found a highly significant effect for the presence of larvae. Atkins (1998) reported 500-750 m² as typical pond size for Triturus cristatus in Great Britain. A minimal pond size of 50 m² and a minimal pond depth of 50 cm are given as key figures for the whole superspecies, with T. carnifex being the species with the highest ecological amplitude (Arntzen 2003). In areas with high densities of Crested newt populations, pond size and depth play an important role, because there are simply more ponds to choose from. For Crested newt larvae there is some evidence that intermediate pond sizes may be favourable (Van Buskirk 2005). In Salzburg these features have no significant effects on their presence. Perhaps here the low number of ponds forces them to take what they can find. The manipulation of ponds by means of fish introduction is one of the major causes for population declines throughout many parts of the distribution range of Crested newts (Thiesmeier & Kupfer 2000). This habitat variable showed no significantly negative effect in our study. Possible explanations might be that on the one hand introduction of fish into most of our studied ponds happened very recently and the number of fish is very low in some cases. Species richness In the province of Salzburg ponds occupied by Crested newts in most instances represent aquatic habitats of high value for amphibians in general. We observed significant differences in amphibian species richness between occupied and unoccupied ponds. Especially the Smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris) and the Tree frog (Hyla arborea), both listed as endangered in the current Red List (Kyek & Maletzky 2006), obviously need similar habitat features in our region. This fact can also be observed vice versa, as a practical conservation project in the years 2002 and 2003 showed. Two of our surveyed ponds (Freimoos 2 and Freimoos 3, see Tab. 1) were created especially for the needs of Tree frogs during a translocation project and were colonised by Crested newts one year after the ponds were created (Kyek et al. in press). Conclusions and implications for future programmes Crested newts (Triturus cristatus superspecies) are at the uppermost level of legal protection in Austria, underlying European (EU habitats directive), national (national Red List) and regional (species protection decree, nature conservation law) regulations. As they are listed in Annex II and IV of the EU habitats directive, the establishment of special protected areas (Natura 2000) as well as monitoring programmes and enhancement measures for aquatic and terrestrial habitats are demanded. Nevertheless a comparably strong decline of population numbers could be observed for no other amphibian species during recent decades and no protected areas have been declared for the needs of these species. At the end of 2005 no occupied Crested newt pond is documented within the range of Natura 2000 areas in Salzburg (Kyek & Maletzky 2006). The effective conservation status of the Crested newt species (Triturus cristatus, T. carnifex) in this area is critical and the high degree of legal protection does not appear to be reflected in conservation benefit. Even intact and frequently reproducing populations show unfavourable conservation status in terms of population sizes, quality of the terrestrial habitat and degree of isolation (Maletzky unpublished data). We strongly call for the initiation of measures to avoid a further decline of these species, not least due to their high significance as indicators of amphibian richness and their great value for science, being located in an area where two species are occurring narrowly sympatric and hybrid populations exist (e.g. Freytag, 1978, Arntzen 2003, Maletzky unpublished data). Crested newts in this area largely depend on artificial ponds. The focus of future conservation efforts must lie in the creation of pond networks, including new artificial ponds as well as the enhancement of old ponds and the parallel development of migration corridors. For aiding as many species as possible, a number of connected smaller ponds may be preferable compared with single large ones (Oertli et al. 2002). Furthermore new ponds should be placed in reachable distances to existing populations and as isolated as possible from human infrastructure preventing the introduction of allochthonous fish and rubbish (Williams et al. 1999). Natural variability of carbon dioxide and net epilimnetic production in the surface waters of boreal lakes of different sizes Carol A. Kelly¹ University of Manitoba, Department of Microbiology, Winnipeg, Manitoba R3T 2N2, Canada Everett Fee,² Patricia S. Ramlal,³ John W. M. Rudd, Raymond H. Hesslein, Cory Anema, and Eva U. Schindler Freshwater Institute, Department of Fisheries and Oceans, 501 University Crescent, Winnipeg, Manitoba R3T 2N6, Canada Abstract The variability of surface water carbon dioxide concentration, or partial pressure (\( pCO_2 \)), was studied in 11 lakes of greatly varying size (2.4 ha up to 8 million ha) in Northwest Ontario, Canada. Six of these lakes were chosen to be as similar as possible in all respects except surface area (the Northwest Ontario Lake Size Series [NOLSS], which range from 88 to 35,000 ha). Spatial and temporal variability of \( pCO_2 \) within a single lake was no greater in the larger lakes than in the smaller lakes. Interannual variability was significant and synchronous, which indicates that weather patterns were important and affected the different lakes within the region in a similar manner. However, annual \( pCO_2 \) averages were not related to annual differences in planktonic photosynthetic activity, measured by \( ^{14}CO_2 \) fixation. In the six NOLSS lakes, there was not a significant relationship of average \( pCO_2 \) with lake size. For all 11 lakes, however, there was a significant negative correlation of \( pCO_2 \) with lake size, which was likely due to several characteristics of the very small and very large lakes that covaried with size. The larger lakes were deeper and had longer water residence times and lower DOC, which suggests lower CO\(_2\) production from allochthonous organic carbon inputs. Also, the ratio of epilimnetic sediment area/epilimnetic volume (\( A_e/V_e \)) was smaller in the larger lakes, which likely resulted in lower rates of recycling of fixed carbon to CO\(_2\) during summer stratification. Measurement of dissolved CO\(_2\) in the surface waters of lakes is as useful as measurement of dissolved oxygen in determining net biological activity in lakes, especially when examining interactions between lakes and their watersheds (Kling et al. 1991; Dillon and Molot 1997). For example, the finding that average CO\(_2\) concentrations in many lakes are above atmospheric equilibrium indicates that allochthonous contributions to lake metabolism often exceed net autochthonous fixation (Cole et al. 1994). This link with watersheds is demonstrated, in a series of Wisconsin lakes, by the positive correlation of surface water CO\(_2\) with the ratio of drainage area to lake area, and with the extent of wetland area surrounding the lake (Hope et al. 1996). Artificial lakes (reservoirs) tend to have higher CO\(_2\) concentrations than natural lakes due to decomposition of flooded vegetation or peat, which could also be considered “allochthonous” carbon sources (Duchemin et al. 1995; Kelly et al. 1997). Where degradation of allochthonous carbon is small, or quantifiable, measurements of CO\(_2\) can give information about the extent of use of autochthonous carbon, i.e., the fraction of photosynthetically fixed CO\(_2\) that is respired after fixation by the algae, grazers, and the rest of the lake’s biota. In addition to biological processes within lakes that affect CO\(_2\), external inputs via streams or groundwater inflows contribute dissolved CO\(_2\) (Kratz et al. 1997) and bicarbonate ions (HCO\(_3^-\)) that can be converted to CO\(_2\) after entering lakes (Dillon and Molot 1997). It is difficult to distinguish between inorganic and organic allochthonous sources of CO\(_2\), but the combination of dissolved oxygen measurement with CO\(_2\) measurements is a promising approach because organic degradation consumes oxygen, whereas inorganic inputs should have no effect on oxygen (Carignan 1998). Previous studies have examined the diel (Sellers et al. 1995) or seasonal variability of CO\(_2\) concentrations in surface waters (Hesslein et al. 1990; Cole et al. 1994) of one or a few lakes. Geographic variability has also been studied, with the data set including a wide variety of lakes, but with few data points from each lake (Cole et al. 1994). The study reported here is the first to carry out long-term (8 yr), regular interval measurements on a fairly large set of lakes in one geographic location and to include measurements of photosynthesis and other parameters that can be used to understand patterns in CO\(_2\). These lakes are generally remote, with minimal anthropogenic impacts. At the core of the study were six remote boreal lakes, the northwest Ontario lake size series (NOLSS, Fee and Hecky 1992). These lakes were chosen to be similar in most characteristics except for surface area, which ranged from 88 to 35,000 ha. We also studied five additional Ontario lakes, extending the size range down to 2.4 ha and up to over 8 million ha.
